title: Imagining Trajectories for Anomaly Detection in Reinforcement Learning from Images
abstract: Abstract Detecting anomalous inputs is a critical prerequisite for the safe deployment of reinforcement learning (RL) agents in real-world environments. Although anomaly detection (AD) has been extensively studied in other domains, its application to reinforcement learning remains challenging due to high-dimensional sensory observations and complex temporal dependencies. Existing approaches in this setting are limited and often rely on access to internal representations of trained agents, creating an undesirable coupling between policy and safety mechanisms. In this work, we propose ITRM, a novel approach to anomaly detection in visual reinforcement learning that is fully agent-agnostic and does not require access to policy internals. Our method is based on the observation that deviations from nominal environment dynamics can be identified through discrepancies in the latent representations of a learned world model. Specifically, we leverage predictive components of a recurrent state-space model to generate deterministic latent embeddings that serve as normative references for anomaly detection. Anomalies are detected by comparing predicted latent features against a reference set of nominal embeddings using a similarity-based criterion. Operating in the world model’s latent space allows the detector to capture semantically meaningful deviations. Extensive empirical evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong detection performance. On the Anomaly-Gym benchmark, our method outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average AUROC of 0.853 and an FPR95 of 0.279.

title: Rényi Entanglement of Purification Is Non-additive
abstract: Entanglement of purification is a fundamental measure of total correlations whose additivity remains unresolved. We study its additivity for classical states on two qubits at different Rényi orders. For every $α\in[0,1)$, we prove nonadditivity within this family, witnessed by two copies of a single state. We first solve the one-copy optimization exactly for the entire family at every Rényi order. We then restrict the two-copy optimization to a natural finite set of purifications and exhibit one whose entropy is strictly below the product value. In contrast, for $α\in[2,\infty]$ we prove additivity under tensor products within this family. The interval $α\in[1,2)$, including the von Neumann case $α=1$, remains open, and we conjecture additivity there throughout the same family.

title: Kerr nonlinearity and three-wave mixing in superconducting resonators hosting Al-InAs weak links
abstract: Nonlinear microwave resonators are a versatile tool in quantum information processing, enabling parametric amplification, continuous variable quantum computing, and engineered mode interactions. Many of these applications especially benefit from cubic nonlinearities enabling three-wave mixing; at the same time, they are limited by quartic nonlinearities giving rise to undesired Kerr effects. A recurrent challenge is therefore to engineer resonators with a finite cubic nonlinearity while suppressing quartic terms. Here, we investigate a superconducting resonator hosting two weak links fabricated from an aluminum-capped indium arsenide nanowire. We characterize the Kerr nonlinearity as a function of magnetic flux and gate bias, showing that it can be tuned to zero with either control parameter. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate three-wave mixing in a semiconductor-superconductor hybrid device, establishing nonzero cubic nonlinearity. An effective model based on Andreev bound states qualitatively captures the observed trends. Our results validate semiconductor-superconductor hybrid devices as a promising platform for tunable nonlinear superconducting circuits, with applications in parametric amplification, quantum control of bosonic modes, and engineering interactions between microwave modes.

title: Gen-TAS: A Generative AI-Aided Hardware-Software Task Allocation Framework for FPGA-GPP Heterogeneous Systems
abstract: FPGA-GPP heterogeneous systems combine software flexibility with the performance and energy efficiency of reconfigurable hardware. However, determining which application tasks should execute on the GPP or FPGA requires extensive expertise and design-space exploration, particularly when user objectives vary across latency, communication, resource utilisation, and power. This paper proposes Gen-TAS, a knowledge-grounded LLM framework for user-specific FPGA-GPP task allocation. By combining task-graph analysis with RAG, Gen-TAS grounds LLM reasoning in historical implementation knowledge and generates multiple explainable strategies tailored to the specified objectives. Human-in-the-loop selection and a deterministic backend connect LLM-generated decisions to reproducible FPGA SoC implementations. Experiments on CNN and SDR workloads across multiple LLMs demonstrate stable, requirement-driven allocation. Under latency-oriented objectives, implementations following the selected strategies achieve speedups of up to 2.45$\times$ and 92.53$\times$, respectively, relative to the corresponding all-GPP baselines while other objectives select strategies that trade some acceleration performance for FPGA-GPP communication, resource utilisation, or FPGA power.

title: CommerceVibe: Learning to Design E-Commerce Creatives as Executable Visual Code via Dual-Feedback Reinforcement Learning
abstract: High-quality e-commerce creatives are essential for presenting products and conveying marketing messages. Recent diffusion models enable scalable creative generation and produce visually compelling images, but their flattened raster outputs often contain distorted text and inconsistent product details, requiring refinement before deployment. Moreover, without explicit structure, the resulting creatives are difficult to edit and reuse, while complex design requirements remain challenging to encode as verifiable training signals. To address these challenges, we present CommerceVibe, which represents creatives as executable visual code and formulates generation as conditional HTML/CSS program synthesis. Given product images, design requirements, and product information, it produces renderable, editable, and reusable creatives. title: Quantum Computation Security Based on Quantum Demagnetization
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to achieving high-security distributed computing by leveraging the principles of quantum demagnetization. Current distributed computing security strategies predominantly rely on cryptographic techniques, which are increasingly vulnerable to attacks from quantum computers. This research introduces a system architecture that decomposes computational tasks into multiple quantum sub-programs and employs quantum demagnetization to guarantee the independence and security of these sub-programs, thus mitigating the risks of malicious attacks and data breaches. The core claim is the utilization of quantum demagnetization to construct a highly secure distributed computing architecture. The key mechanism involves partitioning computational tasks into independent quantum subprograms, ensuring their security through quantum demagnetization, thereby preventing unauthorized access and data leakage. This approach represents a fundamentally new security paradigm, offering resilience against quantum threats that traditional cryptographic methods cannot effectively address. The system's architecture is designed for scalability and adaptability, offering a robust solution for sensitive distributed computing applications. Mathematical formulations and key concepts are presented to demonstrate the theoretical underpinnings of the proposed system.

title: Adaptive Quantum Annealing for Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: This paper presents an adaptive quantum annealing algorithm designed to improve the performance of quantum annealing in solving combinatorial optimization problems. Traditional quantum annealing relies on a fixed annealing schedule, which may not be optimal for all problems. This work introduces a novel approach that utilizes reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust the annealing parameters during the annealing process, based on the observed progress towards a solution. The algorithm learns an optimal annealing schedule by interacting with the quantum annealing system, maximizing the probability of finding a good solution within a given time limit. We demonstrate the theoretical framework and outline the core components of the adaptive algorithm, highlighting its potential advantages over conventional fixed-schedule quantum annealing. The key performance metric is the solution quality (e.g., objective function value) achieved after annealing. The algorithm's effectiveness is evaluated through conceptual analysis and design considerations. This approach aims to bridge the gap between the theoretical potential of quantum annealing and its practical application in solving real-world combinatorial optimization challenges.

title: Non-Homogeneous Data Self-Supervised Learning Methods
abstract: This paper investigates the challenges posed by non-homogeneous data in self-supervised learning (SSL) and proposes a novel framework to address these issues. Traditional SSL methods often struggle when data originates from diverse sources, possessing varying levels of quality, noise, and label distributions. This research focuses on designing self-supervised tasks that effectively leverage the inherent properties of non-homogeneous data, such as contrastive learning, generative modeling, and predictive forecasting. The core claim is to develop a method capable of enhancing model learning capabilities on such datasets. The proposed mechanism utilizes data-specific characteristics to generate suitable self-supervised tasks, ultimately learning robust and meaningful data representations. The presented approach aims to improve the performance of SSL models in scenarios where data heterogeneity is a significant factor, offering a pathway to more effective learning from diverse data sources. We explore the mathematical underpinnings of the proposed method and demonstrate its potential through theoretical analysis and conceptual design.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Secure Aggregation and Differential Privacy
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without direct data sharing. However, traditional FL schemes are vulnerable to privacy attacks, particularly model inversion attacks, which can reveal sensitive information about the underlying data. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated learning framework that integrates secure aggregation and differential privacy to mitigate these risks. The system utilizes secure aggregation techniques, such as homomorphic encryption, to protect individual model updates during the aggregation process. Simultaneously, differential privacy mechanisms are employed to limit the amount of information leaked about individual clients' data. The decentralized nature of the framework enhances robustness and scalability. This approach significantly strengthens the privacy guarantees of FL while maintaining model accuracy and efficiency. The core claim of this work is that enhancing security and privacy is crucial for the wider adoption of federated learning. The proposed mechanism combines secure aggregation and differential privacy in a decentralized federated learning framework.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing for Secure Multi-Party Computation
abstract: This paper explores the application of hyperdimensional computing (HDC) to secure multi-party computation (SMPC). Traditional SMPC methods often suffer from high computational overhead and communication costs. HDC, characterized by its data compression, robustness to noise, and efficient vector operations, provides a promising alternative. We propose a framework for mapping computation tasks onto HDC vectors, leveraging HDC's properties to enable secure aggregation and computation while minimizing the amount of information exchanged between parties. The core claim is that HDC's unique characteristics can significantly improve the efficiency of SMPC protocols. We present a conceptual model and discuss key considerations for implementing this approach, highlighting potential advantages over existing SMPC techniques. The presented approach demonstrates the potential for significantly reducing computational complexity and communication costs in secure multi-party computation.

title: Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing for Complex System Dynamics
abstract: Reservoir computing is a promising technique for modeling complex, non-linear dynamics, yet its effectiveness is often limited by the inherent constraints of classical neural networks. This work proposes a novel approach, termed Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing, which leverages fundamental principles of quantum mechanics – specifically superposition and entanglement – to dramatically enhance the representational capacity of the reservoir. The core idea involves constructing a "Quantum Reservoir" comprised of interconnected nodes, each operating in a superposition of states, governed by stochastic differential equations influenced by quantum mechanical concepts. This framework allows for richer, more nuanced representations of system dynamics compared to traditional reservoir computing. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach, focusing on the mapping between quantum states and reservoir nodes and the dynamics generated by these systems. Preliminary analysis suggests significant potential for improved performance in modeling complex systems, representing a substantial advancement in the field. The key contributions of this paper include the formalization of this quantum-inspired reservoir model, the derivation of associated stochastic differential equations, and an initial exploration of its potential benefits.

title: Cognitive Computing with Bayesian Networks and Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive architecture that leverages the strengths of Bayesian Networks (BNs) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to address the limitations of traditional cognitive architectures. The core claim is that traditional architectures struggle to effectively integrate prior knowledge and learn from experience. Our approach combines BNs for representing and reasoning with prior knowledge, and DRL for learning optimal policies from data within dynamic environments. The system aims to achieve robust reasoning, planning, and adaptive behavior. We formalize the architecture using a hybrid framework, presenting the key components and their interactions. This architecture offers a more powerful approach to cognitive modeling, enabling systems to learn effectively and reason intelligently. Specifically, we define the core components: a Bayesian Network module for knowledge representation and inference, a Deep Reinforcement Learning module for policy learning, and a communication interface facilitating interaction between the two modules. We outline the mathematical foundations underpinning the system, including the probability distributions within the BN, the reward functions used in DRL, and the algorithms employed for both inference and learning. The architecture's potential impact on areas such as robotics, autonomous systems, and intelligent decision-making is discussed.

title: Robustness of Two-Mode Entanglement in Multi-Mode Interference-Based Quantum Teleportation
abstract: Preserving entanglement during the teleportation of multipartite quantum states is a central challenge in continuous-variable quantum communication, particularly when experimentally feasible finite-dimensional entangled resources are employed. In this work, we investigate whether the entanglement of a two-mode continuous-variable state can be preserved when only one of its modes is teleported through a multimode interferometry-based protocol using a three-dimensional discrete entangled channel. Two representative entangled states, namely the two-mode squeezed vacuum and discrete-modulation states, are considered under both ideal conditions and four standard quantum noise channels: bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping. The protocol is evaluated in terms of teleportation fidelity, success probability, logarithmic negativity, Wigner-function evolution, and state purity to provide a comprehensive assessment of both teleportation quality and entanglement preservation. The results show that, in the absence of noise, the protocol preserves most of the initial entanglement while maintaining high teleportation fidelity. Under noisy conditions, the residual entanglement remains remarkably robust against amplitude-damping and phase-flip noise, whereas bit-flip noise causes the most pronounced degradation. The phase-space structure and purity of the teleported states are likewise largely retained over a broad range of noise strengths. These findings demonstrate that multimode interferometry with finite-dimensional entangled channels provides an effective and noise-resilient approach for preserving continuous-variable entanglement during quantum teleportation, offering a practical route toward realistic quantum communication networks.

title: Enhancing regulatory foresight through weak signal mining: An AI-based micro-topic emergence scoring approach
authors: Bas H. M. van der Velden
abstract: Emerging risks in food and feed safety often manifest through weak, ambiguous signals long before they reach regulatory attention. This paper presents the Weak Signal Miner (WSM), an AI-based, end-to-end pipeline for detecting such early-stage signals within large text corpora. The method combines transformer-based micro-topic modelling, adaptive temporal aggregation, and a recency-and-magnitude scoring scheme to identify rare topics that show disproportionate recent growth. An optional interpretation layer using large language models (LLMs) provides intuitive labels, novelty and severity scores to support expert evaluation without replacing human judgement. Retrospective analyses demonstrate the tool’s effectiveness: the WSM surfaces signals related to Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) contamination (2004–2007) and citrinin in red yeast rice supplements (2010–2017) well before their formal recognition in an EFSA (European Food Safety Authority) opinion. Weak signal mining provides a data-driven complement to expert-based emerging risk identification, by systematically surfacing potential issues that may precede, escape, or only later enter traditional expert information channels and formal institutional processes.

title: Enhancing Solar PV Efficiency through a Digital Twin Framework and Machine Learning Models
abstract: This study develops a Digital Twin for solar power forecasting using an ANN model, aiming to accurately simulate the behavior of a 20W solar panel. The model was trained and evaluated across three datasets: training, validation, and testing, with performance metrics such as Mean Squared Error (MSE) and correlation coefficient (R) used to assess its effectiveness. The results show that the training set achieved an MSE of 8.1715 and an R of 0.9994, the validation set achieved an MSE of 6.8499 and an R of 0.9995, and the test set achieved an MSE of 8.9045 and an R of 0.9994. These metrics indicate strong predictive accuracy across all datasets. The model successfully replicates the power generation behavior of the solar panel, providing reliable forecasts for both seen and unseen data. The model's ability to predict solar power output accurately suggests its potential for real-time monitoring, system optimization, and performance prediction, making it a promising tool for enhancing solar panel operations and efficiency. Through this Digital Twin approach, solar power systems can be better understood, maintained, and optimized, supporting the broader adoption of sustainable energy technologies.

title: Pixel-wise Geo-registration of Drone and Satellite Images
abstract: Pixel-level cross-view geo-registration aims to align a query image (e.g., drone) to a geo-referenced satellite map so that every query pixel can be mapped to real-world GPS coordinates. Despite strong progress in cross-view geo-localization, existing benchmarks largely provide only GPS labels, limiting evaluation to a single coordinate per image and leaving dense geodetic alignment underexplored. We introduce SkyReg, a dataset and standardized benchmark for pixel-level drone-to-satellite geo-registration, providing dense per-pixel geo-location supervision across diverse settings (orthographic and perspective), scene types (urban, landmark-centric, suburban/rural), and camera configurations. Using SkyReg, we evaluate a broad set of baselines spanning retrieval, feature matching, homography-based alignment, and feed-forward 3D reconstruction. Finally, cross-view pairs from SkyReg, we train a geometry-aware reconstruction pipeline that achieves state-of-the-art results,improving performance by a significant margin.

title: Determinant Quantum-Quantum Monte Carlo: Coherent Auxiliary-Field Sampling
abstract: We introduce determinant quantum-quantum Monte Carlo (DQ$^2$MC), a quantum algorithm that lifts the auxiliary-field sampling and averaging at the operational core of determinant quantum Monte Carlo onto a quantum computer. A determinant oracle synthesizes the DQMC amplitudes directly from a block encoding of the single-particle action matrix via quantum singular value transformations, so that the exponentially many Hubbard-Stratonovich weights are never enumerated, precomputed, or stored. Since the fermions are free for fixed auxiliary fields, the construction operates entirely at the single-particle level, requiring $O(\log N_{\mathrm{st}})$ system qubits and no Jordan-Wigner or Bravyi-Kitaev encoding, where $N_{\mathrm{st}}$ is the space-time volume. A full-quantum protocol makes observables interference amplitudes, eliminating the Markov chain and its autocorrelation time altogether; a hybrid quantum-classical protocol retains a constant-size active block of qubits and replaces the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance step with an exact heat-bath draw, so that cluster updates of any size are rejection-free, and passes only classical information between updates, admitting parallel tempering and distributed execution across quantum processors. The circuit-depth scales more favorably with spatial volume than classical DQMC, at the price of a post-selection overhead determined exactly by the largest target probability --- polynomial for smooth distributions, exponential for sharply peaked ones. Finally, the reweighting estimator underlying the fermion sign problem maps exactly onto a quantum weak value, placing the exponential cost of sign-problematic DQMC in precise correspondence with the post-selection overhead of weak-value extraction.

title: Thread-Efficient Decoding for Neural Texture Compression
abstract: Neural texture compression (NTC) achieves higher compression ratios than BCn formats but suffers from GPU thread divergence, which significantly reduces runtime performance. In this work, we propose a shared decoder MLP architecture -- trained with a gradual decoder freezing schedule -- combined with texture clustering to reduce thread divergence by 25%-52% while preserving rendering quality. We evaluate our method on over 500 textures and multiple real rendering scenes, demonstrating up to 8.48x speedup on the Radeon RX 9070 XT GPU compared to non-shared baselines. Our key contributions include: (1) a unified shared decoder architecture that reduces divergence by grouping textures; (2) a training recipe with gradual decoder freezing that improves stability and reconstruction accuracy; (3) a semantic clustering strategy using CLIP embeddings that groups similar textures for effective decoder sharing; and (4) comprehensive performance and ablation studies validating our approach.

title: Analysis of Consumer Impulsive Buying Behavior Towards Usage of Artificial Intelligence on E-commerce Platform
abstract: This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI) influences consumer's spontaneous or unplanned purchases in electronic commerce. The development and increasing use of various types of automated systems in e-commerce such as, but not limited to, chatbots, personalized product recommendation and real-time offers, provide new opportunities for influencing consumer's purchase decisions through automation. By investigating how these AI based tools directly or indirectly affect consumers' psychological states (e.g., convenience, urgency, customization), which stimulate unplanned or emotionally-based purchasing behaviours, this study seeks to contribute to a better understanding of how external AI based stimulus can generate internal response and subsequent behaviour. As part of its methodology, the study uses a mixed methodological design including both an online survey and qualitative interviews to investigate the level at which consumers engage with AI. The study is based upon the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) model; Instant Gratification theory; and Cognitive Dissonance theory, among other psychological models, to examine how the AI generated stimulus leads to internal response and consequently affects the consumer's purchasing behaviour. Therefore, it is expected that AI will have a significant effect on the likelihood of spontaneous purchases due to both promotional activities and customised product recommendations. In addition, younger adults and those who possess greater discretionary income will likely be more susceptible than older adults and lower-income individuals. Ultimately, the purpose of this study is to help companies understand AI's role in their business practices and make informed decisions about ethical AI usage; therefore providing further knowledge regarding the long-term impacts of AI on consumer behaviour.

evidence.title: Analysis of Consumer Impulsive Buying Behavior Towards Usage of Artificial Intelligence on E-commerce Platform
evidence.abstract: This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI) influences consumer's spontaneous or unplanned purchases in electronic commerce. The development and increasing use of various types of automated systems in e-commerce such as, but not limited to, chatbots, personalized product recommendation and real-time offers, provide new opportunities for influencing consumer's purchase decisions through automation. By investigating how these AI based tools directly or indirectly affect consumers' psychological states (e.g., convenience, urgency, customization), which stimulate unplanned or emotionally-based purchasing behaviours, this study seeks to contribute to a better understanding of how external AI based stimulus can generate internal response and subsequent behaviour. As part of its methodology, the study uses a mixed methodological design including both an online survey and qualitative interviews to investigate the level at which consumers engage with AI. The study is based upon the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) model; Instant Gratification theory; and Cognitive Dissonance theory, among other psychological models, to examine how the AI generated stimulus leads to internal response and consequently affects the consumer's purchasing behaviour. Therefore, it is expected that AI will have a significant effect on the likelihood of spontaneous purchases due to both promotional activities and customised product recommendations. In addition, younger adults and those who possess greater discretionary income will likely be more susceptible than older adults and lower-income individuals. title: Understanding public perceptions of waste management: A comparative sentiment analysis using LSTM and IndoBERT
abstract: Background: Waste management remains one of Indonesia’s pressing environmental and social challenges, characterized by increasing waste generation and public dissatisfaction with existing waste-treatment systems. Understanding public sentiment toward waste-management policies and community-based programs is essential for supporting more effective interventions. This study aims to examine public perceptions of waste-management issues in Indonesia and compare the performance of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Indonesian Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (IndoBERT) for sentiment classification. Methods: This study used a dataset of 15,000 public text opinions collected from social media using a crawling technique. The data were manually annotated into three sentiment categories: positive, neutral, and negative. After preprocessing, two sentiment-classification models, LSTM and IndoBERT, were developed and evaluated. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Topic-based sentiment analysis was also conducted to identify public perceptions of major waste-management issues. Findings: The results showed that IndoBERT outperformed LSTM in sentiment classification by capturing contextual meaning and sentiment nuances in Indonesian-language expressions more effectively. Topic-based analysis indicated that community-based initiatives, including waste banks and recycling programs, were generally associated with positive sentiment. In contrast, landfill-related issues were more frequently associated with negative sentiment due to concerns about pollution and poor management. Conclusion: IndoBERT provides a more reliable approach for analyzing public sentiment toward waste-management issues in Indonesia. The findings highlight the importance of understanding public perceptions to strengthen community engagement, improve public communication, and support more effective waste-management policies and programs. Novelty/Originality of this article: The novelty of this study lies in integrating deep learning-based sentiment classification with topic-based sentiment analysis to examine public opinion specifically regarding waste-management strategies in Indonesia. The comparative evaluation of LSTM and IndoBERT also provides empirical insight into the suitability of contextual language models for analyzing Indonesian-language public opinions on waste management.

title: Differential Privacy for Distributed Graph Analytics
abstract: This paper explores the application of differential privacy to the field of distributed graph analytics. Large-scale graph datasets, prevalent in domains like social networks and biological data, often contain sensitive information. Traditional analytical methods on these datasets can expose individuals' private data, raising serious privacy concerns. We propose a novel distributed algorithm designed to mitigate these risks by injecting carefully calibrated noise during the aggregation of graph statistics. This algorithm achieves differential privacy, providing quantifiable guarantees against privacy breaches while maintaining a reasonable level of analytical utility. The core claim is that differential privacy can be effectively applied to distributed graph analytics, offering a robust solution for privacy-preserving analysis of complex network data. The methodology focuses on a practical, scalable approach suitable for real-world distributed environments. We detail the algorithm's design, the mathematical framework underpinning the privacy guarantees, and discuss the trade-offs between privacy and utility.

title: Distributed Proof Verification via Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: The verification of mathematical proofs remains a significant challenge in mathematics and computer science. Manual proof verification is a laborious, subjective, and prone-to-error activity, particularly for complex theorems. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to automate the process of distributed proof verification. The core idea is to evolve a population of proof strategies, represented as mathematical rules and logical steps, iteratively refining them through testing and feedback. The algorithm aims to generate potentially correct proofs and, critically, to identify and eliminate incorrect strategies. Our framework offers a potential solution to the problem of verifying complex proofs, reducing the reliance on human expertise and accelerating the discovery and validation of mathematical results. The system's effectiveness relies on the fitness function, which evaluates the proof based on logical consistency and adherence to the original theorem. This work outlines the architecture, key components, and the evolutionary algorithm design, focusing on the core mechanics of proof generation and verification. The ultimate goal is to establish a robust and efficient system for automated mathematical proof verification.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation with Model-Free Imitation Learning and Bayesian Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to robotic manipulation training leveraging the strengths of model-free imitation learning and Bayesian optimization. Traditional reinforcement learning methods often struggle with the complexity and high sample requirements of robotic tasks. Our approach addresses this challenge by first learning from expert demonstrations via model-free imitation learning. Subsequently, Bayesian optimization is employed to efficiently tune the robot's control parameters, accelerating the learning process and achieving superior performance. The core claim is that combining these techniques drastically reduces the training time and difficulty associated with robotic manipulation. We detail the framework, outlining the integration of both methods and explore the potential for significant advancements in robot control. The presented methodology offers a practical and robust solution for training robots to perform complex manipulation tasks in a significantly reduced timeframe.

title: Probabilistic Verification of Deep Learning Models via Monte Carlo Dropout and Bayesian Inference
abstract: The increasing deployment of deep learning models in critical applications necessitates robust verification methods to ensure their reliability and safety. Traditional verification techniques often rely on exhaustive testing or approximations, which can be computationally expensive or inaccurate. This paper proposes a novel framework for probabilistic verification of deep learning models leveraging the combined power of Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout) and Bayesian inference. The core idea is to generate a distribution of model outputs under various inputs by repeatedly performing forward passes with MC Dropout. Analyzing this distribution allows for a quantitative assessment of the model's uncertainty and provides a means to verify its behavior, specifically focusing on identifying potential vulnerabilities and unexpected outputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a practical methodology for implementing probabilistic verification. The key contribution lies in providing a rigorous and scalable method for assessing the robustness of deep learning models, addressing a critical gap in the current landscape of model validation.

title: AI-supported methods for analysis of unstructured text responses in patient survey in primary healthcare comparing changes over time. (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Free-text responses collected through patient-reported experience measures contain valuable information for healthcare quality improvement. These comments are underused because they are difficult to analyse at scale. Natural language processing (NLP) and AI-supported text-analysis methods offer new possibilities for transforming large volumes of patient comments into structured information. In Sweden, the National Patient Survey (NPS) has collected patient-reported experience data in primary healthcare since 2009, and an open-ended free-text question was introduced in 2017. However, systematic analysis of the free-text responses for quality improvement remains limited. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to examine whether AI-supported text-analysis techniques can be used to transform free-text responses from the Swedish NPS into structured information with potential relevance for quality improvement in primary healthcare. The specific objectives were to identify the aspects of care patients comment on, assess the sentiment expressed toward these aspects, and explore how aspects and associated sentiments change over time. METHODS The study used routinely collected free-text responses from the Swedish NPS in primary healthcare. Established NLP methods were applied. First, unsupervised topic modelling was used to identify candidate themes in the patient comments. Second, rule-based dictionary methods were used to extract predefined aspects of care. Third, a pre-trained transformer-based model was applied to classify sentiment associated with patient comments. The resulting structured information was used to describe the distribution of aspects of care, sentiment patterns, and changes over time. RESULTS 24 unique aspect categories were identified out of 8,328 documents which were included in the analysis. The fine-tuned KB-BERT model achieved an overall accuracy of 90% on the validation set, with moderate-to-high F1-scores for several key aspect categories, including staff turnover (F1=0.94), follow-up (F1=0.83), emergency care (F1=0.84), and language (F1=0.89). Manual validation showed that 65% of the texts were judged to be correctly classified, while 35% exhibited some degree of misclassification. CONCLUSIONS AI-supported analysis of free-text responses from patient surveys has the potential to complement structured patient-reported experience measures by making large volumes of qualitative feedback more accessible for analysis and quality improvement. By combining topic modelling, aspect extraction, and sentiment classification, this study explores a scalable approach for analysing routinely collected patient comments in Swedish primary healthcare. CLINICALTRIAL n/a

title: DLOps
abstract: DLOps (Deep Learning Operations) is an extension of MLOps (Machine Learning Operations) in which the focus is on huge datasets, computationally intensive predictions, black-box natured model prediction, and continuously evolving nature of the prediction model with dynamic data. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly being embedded into the model development phase rather than applied only as a posthoc step. The integration of explainability at each and every stage of DL model development enhances transparency, trust, and debugging efficiency, ensuring that the model’s behavior aligns with human reasoning and domain knowledge. This chapter discusses key strategies for embedding explainability directly into DL pipelines, which will enhance DLOps in an interpretable and reliable way of DL model development.

title: Application of Fuzzy Set Theory to AI and Machine Learning Domain
abstract: Fuzzy set theory has emerged as a significant technique in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for effectively handling the inherent uncertainty and imprecision in real-world data. This abstract explores the significant impact of fuzzy set theory on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies, offering a comprehensive overview of its applications and benefits. The incorporation of fuzzy set theory into AI and ML systems improves their efficacy by including the concept of partial membership and granular boundaries. This enables them to precisely describe and analyze information that is confusing, ambiguous, and uncertain. AI systems can employ fuzzy logic-based inference mechanisms, such as fuzzy rule-based systems and fuzzy clustering algorithms, to improve decision-making and extract important insights from complex and ambiguous datasets with increased accuracy and robustness. Moreover, the integration of fuzzy set theory with deep learning frameworks has led to the development of hybrid models that can proficiently handle both structured and unstructured data effortlessly. This abstract also explores the challenges and future directions in applying fuzzy set theory in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) domains, including the need for algorithms capable of handling large-scale problems, the ability to interpret the outcomes, and the resilience against adversarial attacks. Generally, the integration of fuzzy set theory represents a fundamental shift in how machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) systems comprehend and examine ambiguity. This modification creates opportunities for the advancement of intelligence that is flexible enough, resilient, and capable of imitating human-like behavior.

title: Fidelity Is Not Enough: Dispatch-Level Instrumentation for Agentic Datasheet Extraction
abstract: One model passed our fidelity check without ever opening the datasheet. We found it while qualifying models for an internal extraction service: a structured-output constraint had silently disabled tool use, and the model answered anyway, with fabricated source text. Only the per-tool trace exposed it. Fidelity -- whether an extracted value matches the source -- is the standard measure for agentic document extraction, and it scores that run a success. We therefore log every tool call in an agentic benchmark of 25 hand-curated claims over three components, with 12 more on a fourth, 37 in all. From that dispatch record we build two instruments: a rule-based failure-attribution classifier, and a silent-failure detector whose two rules check only which tools were called, never the extracted value. The detector raises no flag on 207 clean fidelity-passing extractions across three model families, and recovers all 50 planted faults that withhold exactly the tools its rules check. The two results are not symmetric: the first bounds the false-positive rate, the second is recall by construction, and detection power against runs that call their tools and still answer wrongly is unmeasured. A second, independent oracle, a causal chamber that tests whether the datasheet's claims hold under physical measurement, is intentionally partial: it confirms only what the apparatus can exercise, a verifiable envelope of 2 of those 37 claims, and we give a taxonomy of why the rest are not physically gradable. Under a controlled perturbation, fidelity passes throughout while the chamber verdict flips exactly at the measurement uncertainty. Across three deployed model stacks (one destabilised by its serving stack, not by any capability gap) the tool layer buys portability and observability rather than accuracy, and earns its premium only once a document outgrows the context window.

title: Quantum-Safe Cybersecurity Strategies: Policy Frameworks for Protecting Government Data and National Critical Systems
abstract: The anticipated development of cryptographically relevant quantum computing presents a strategic challenge to governments because contemporary public-sector information systems depend extensively on cryptographic mechanisms for confidentiality, authentication, integrity, and secure communication. The principal difficulty is not limited to replacing existing cryptographic algorithms; rather, it concerns the coordinated transformation of national information infrastructures, institutional policies, data-protection practices, procurement procedures, and long-term security architectures. This research and review article develops a policy-oriented framework for quantum-safe cybersecurity in government environments. The study adopts a conceptual methodology that synthesizes the supplied literature on predictive modeling, statistical decision-making, machine learning, and quantum-resistant national-security policy. Although several supplied studies originate in pharmaceutical stability prediction rather than cybersecurity, their methodological emphasis on prediction, modeling, optimization, and risk-oriented decision processes provides transferable analytical foundations for constructing migration and prioritization mechanisms. The proposed framework integrates cryptographic inventory, risk classification, data sensitivity assessment, migration prioritization, algorithm-agility requirements, governance controls, validation mechanisms, and continuous monitoring. The analysis indicates that quantum-safe transformation should be treated as a national digital-resilience program rather than as an isolated cryptographic upgrade. The paper further identifies implementation challenges involving legacy systems, interoperability, institutional coordination, resource allocation, and uncertainty concerning future quantum capabilities. The resulting framework provides a structured basis for government agencies to prioritize critical assets, reduce exposure to future cryptographic compromise, and establish adaptive cybersecurity governance.

title: Taal in constructie. Een constructivistisch perspectief van taal in machines versus mensen.
abstract: This dissertation starts from important insights derived from usage-based constructionist theories, according to which language is acquired in the form of constructions, multidimensional form-function pairings containing information from the lexical and syntactico-semantic levels simultaneously. Given their nature and flexibility, constructions can be used to model linguistic structures of different lengths and types, and, importantly, to analyse the mechanisms behind language learning, processing and use. Based on these theoretical underpinnings, this project adopts computational construction grammars, first analysed and categorised in detail through a systematic literature review, to model and study how language is learned and produced by humans and machines, in both first and second language contexts. To fill one of the largest gaps in current computational models for language learning, two novel algorithms are introduced that process and learn directly from unsegmented character sequences, discovering constructions bottom-up from continuous input and, therefore, bringing computational models closer to human usage-based acquisition mechanisms. Next to this methodological contribution, shifting from language learning and processing to use and production, this dissertation presents a constructionist solution to the real-world issue of AI detection, for which educators in particular need linguistically grounded and interpretable solutions. Constructionist features are applied at corpus scale to L2 learner essays and LLM-generated counterparts, demonstrating that human writers exhibit modal-epistemic hedging and diverse abstract grammatical templates that reflect usage-based acquisition and appear across different levels of competence. On the contrary, LLMs produce nominally dense patterns shaped by next-token prediction and display a more limited constructional repertoire, both in terms of abstract patterns and lexical realisations. These differences remain detectable across model families, proficiency levels and AI-assisted revision conditions. Overall, this dissertation provides evidence in support of the fact that the constructional lens can not only serve to model language in detail, across its different phases and first and second language users, but also to scrutinise its components, below and beyond the word level, serving tasks such as AI detection in educational contexts, where human and machine language distinctions are key. The key outcome is, thus, that human and machine language differences cannot simply be traced back to different vocabularies or styles, but need to be inspected by considering the building blocks of language, constructions, and in particular, how these are used during the constructing phases of language itself, influenced by the processes and mechanisms behind it.

Overall, this dissertation provides evidence in support of the fact that the constructional lens can not only serve to model language in detail, across its different phases and first and second language users, but also to scrutinise its components, below and beyond the word level, serving tasks such as AI detection in educational contexts, where human and machine language distinctions are key. The key outcome is, thus, that human and machine language differences cannot simply be traced back to different vocabularies or styles, but need to be inspected by considering the building blocks of language, constructions, and in particular, how these are used during the constructing phases of language itself, influenced by the processes and mechanisms behind it.

title: Information-Theoretic Proofs of Robustness for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to assessing the robustness of neural networks by leveraging information-theoretic principles. We propose a framework that utilizes mutual information and entropy to quantify information loss during adversarial attacks. The core idea is to derive probabilistic guarantees for attack success based on these information-theoretic measures, moving beyond purely empirical evaluation methods. Specifically, we formulate bounds on the probability of a successful adversarial attack, directly linked to the information retained within the network's representation space. This work establishes a rigorous, information-theoretic foundation for quantifying and understanding neural network robustness, offering a potentially more reliable and insightful approach compared to existing methods. This paper offers a theoretical framework, providing a deeper understanding of how adversarial perturbations affect network behavior. We introduce key metrics—mutual information and entropy—to analyze the vulnerability of neural networks. The core contribution lies in deriving quantifiable bounds on the probability of successful attacks based on these information-theoretic measures, allowing for a more precise evaluation of robustness.

title: Based on Multi-Layer Neural Networks for Quantum State Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum state simulation utilizing multi-layer neural networks. Traditional methods of quantum simulation, particularly those based on solving the Schrödinger equation, face significant computational challenges, especially for complex quantum systems with numerous qubits. This research proposes a framework where a multi-layer neural network is trained to approximate the dynamics of a quantum system, effectively mimicking the behavior of a quantum system without explicitly solving the underlying equations. The core of this method lies in the neural network's inherent ability to learn complex, non-linear mappings, allowing it to represent the time evolution dictated by the Schrödinger equation. We explore the architecture of the network, focusing on its ability to capture the intricate correlations within quantum states. The results demonstrate the potential for significantly faster and more efficient quantum state simulation compared to conventional approaches, offering a viable path toward simulating larger and more complex quantum systems.

title: Quantum Entanglement States Protected by Topology and Information Storage
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to enhancing the stability and storage capabilities of quantum entanglement states by leveraging topological protection. The core idea centers around manipulating the geometric topology of quantum systems to create a protective barrier against decoherence, a primary source of quantum information loss. We propose a framework where specific topological structures are engineered to shield entangled states, significantly extending their coherence times and improving their resilience to environmental perturbations. The theoretical framework outlines the design principles and mathematical formalism for achieving robust topological protection of entanglement. We explore the potential for utilizing this method in practical quantum information storage applications. The key elements involve constructing systems with non-trivial topological invariants, which effectively isolate the entangled states from external disturbances. This work provides a foundational understanding and a potential pathway towards developing more reliable and scalable quantum storage devices.

title: Graph Representation Learning via Latent Topological Diffusion
abstract: Graph representation learning aims to learn effective embeddings for nodes in a graph, enabling downstream tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively capture the intricate and complex topological relationships inherent in graph data. This paper introduces a novel approach – Latent Topological Diffusion – that addresses this limitation by explicitly modelling diffusion processes on the graph, guided by a learned latent topological field. This field iteratively updates node representations based on their local neighborhood structure, effectively propagating topological information across the graph. The core claim is that by incorporating this diffusion mechanism, we can better capture long-range dependencies and complex graph structures. We present a detailed formulation of the method, including the diffusion equation, the latent field, and the learning objective. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through theoretical analysis and a comprehensive evaluation on benchmark graph datasets. The key innovations lie in the explicit modeling of topological diffusion and the use of a learned latent topological field to guide the process.

title: Scalable Gaussian processes and active learning for emulator design in solar wind simulation
abstract: In this thesis we discuss emulator design for solar wind simulators. Our work focuses on two areas. Firstly, we focus on scaling Gaussian process regression to work well on simulator grids with millions of points. We accomplish this by extending existing work on Kronecker product covariance based algorithms to work efficiently with a dataset larger than working memory. Secondly, we implement and experiment with existing acquisition functions for active learning in the large data regime found in simulators. We find encouraging, though not definitive, results in favour of the expected predictive information gain acquisition function, particularly when the predictive distribution is well specified. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first time that Gaussian process regression has been applied at this scale in solar wind modelling, the first time that these acquisition functions have been implemented at this scale for Gaussian process models, and the first time that active learning has been applied to the problem of emulator design for the solar wind.

title: DPTM-DT: Dual-Pretrained Transformer Multitask Representation Learning for Drug-Target Prediction
abstract: Drug-target relation prediction supports candidate screening, drug repositioning, and mechanism analysis. Existing models often use incomplete drug or protein representations, model cross-modal interactions shallowly, or train affinity regression and interaction classification separately, although these tasks describe closely related views of the same drug-target pair. This paper presents DPTM-DT, a dual-pretrained Transformer framework for multitask drug-target prediction. DPTM-DT combines GROVER molecular graph embeddings, ESM protein language-model embeddings, and CTD physicochemical descriptors, then exchanges drug-target information through bidirectional cross-modal attention. A shared pair representation is used for continuous affinity regression, high-affinity binary classification, and six-level affinity classification. Experiments on Davis and KIBA cover random 80/20 and DeepDTA-style standard splits. On the random 80/20 split, DPTM-DT achieves MSE/CI values of 0.193/0.917 on Davis and 0.120/0.918 on KIBA. It also reports binary AUPR/MCC values of 0.727/0.654 and 0.798/0.689, and six-class Macro-F1/Top-2 values of 0.800/0.932 and 0.815/0.962 on Davis and KIBA, respectively. Across the reported regression, binary classification, and multiclass classification settings, DPTM-DT achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods. Results under the standard split show the same relative trend. Ablations indicate that dual target representation, gated fusion, and cross-modal attention each contribute to the final performance. Code and supplementary materials are available at: anonymous.4open.science/r/DPCM-DT-74E0.

title: Direct Adaptive Certification of High-Dimensional Entanglement with Bell Tests
abstract: Entangled photons play a crucial role in quantum applications, and determining and characterising their entanglement is vital to using them effectively. High-dimensional entangled states offer richer possibilities, but their additional measurement degrees of freedom make them increasingly demanding to characterise. However, adaptive Bell-test methods based on complex simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (CSPSA) have so far focused mainly on qubits. Here we numerically investigate a Bell-inequality-violation-based method for detecting entanglement in unknown quantum states. We extend CSPSA to high-dimensional Bell testing by using the Collins-Gisin-Linden-Massar-Popescu (CGLMP) inequality for bipartite qudits. The resulting protocol can detect Bell-nonlocal correlations in unknown entangled states, whether pure or mixed, without first reconstructing their density matrix. Using 100 optimisation iterations in each of 100 independent finite-shot runs per number of dimensions d, we demonstrate certified CGLMP violations throughout d=2-8. For isotropic mixed states tested at a visibility of just 0.05 above the standard-Fourier violation threshold, we likewise observe confidence-certified CGLMP violations throughout the range of d studied. We compare this direct stochastic approach with quantum state tomography, the standard method for characterising an unknown state. In the matched benchmark, CSPSA uses fewer measurement configurations per attempt from d=6, whereas tomography requires fewer detected pairs per certified result through d=8. We also derive the phase dependence of the CGLMP parameter and clarify the features of its landscape that govern the adaptive search. Because the measurement-setting cost of each CSPSA iteration is independent of dimension, the method offers a particularly attractive route to the certification of high-dimensional entanglement.

title: Under-Mattress Temporal Sensing for Next-Day Agitation Risk Scoring in Dementia Wards
abstract: Agitation fluctuates over short time horizons in people living with dementia, yet continuous physiological information for anticipating next-day risk is limited. We assessed whether contactless under-mattress signals from the preceding night inform next-day agitation risk and whether preserving minute-level temporal structure improves performance over conventional nightly summaries. We analyzed 423 patient-nights from 65 subjects in a specialized hospital dementia unit using two under-mattress sensing systems. A unified four-paradigm benchmark compared nightly handcrafted summaries, three-period handcrafted features, full-night sequence modeling, and sliding-window multiple-instance learning. Source-specific preprocessing and five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation were used, with performance estimated from pooled out-of-fold predictions. Evaluation included discrimination, calibration, fixed-threshold metrics, and a comparison of period-signal attribution patterns across two temporal models. Full-night sequence modeling achieved the highest discrimination (AUROC, 0.692; AUPRC, 0.849) and balanced accuracy (0.658). Both minute-level pipelines had higher AUROC than nightly summaries, but differences from three-period handcrafted features were uncertain. Cross-model attribution prioritized activity, heart rate, and respiratory rate during the core overnight period. Calibration remained limited. The preceding night's signals supported modest next-day risk discrimination, with minute-level temporal modeling outperforming nightly summaries. Prospective calibration and external validation are needed before use in individual care decisions. This patient-grouped benchmark identifies contactless overnight sensing as a promising biomedical engineering direction for agitation-risk research in hospitalized dementia cohorts.

title: Encoding strategies for quantum enhanced fluid simulations: opportunities and challenges
abstract: Abstract Quantum computing has emerged as a powerful potential accelerator for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but whether this promise can be realized in practice depends on how fluid information is encoded on quantum hardware. This review provides an architecture-agnostic assessment of encoding strategies for quantum-enhanced fluid simulation, focusing on the trade-offs they impose on state preparation, measurement, boundary treatment, nonlinear dynamics, and temporal evolution. We examine the principal encoding paradigms used in the literature and relate them to representative quantum algorithms for fluid simulation. Through these examples, we show that encoding choices fundamentally shape both the algorithm itself and also the practical feasibility of quantum CFD (QCFD). For example, highly compact encodings can offer attractive asymptotic advantages but might introduce severe bottlenecks in readout, state preparation, and nonlinear processing, whereas less compact representations may simplify interactions and improve compatibility with analog and near-term hardware. No single encoding is universally optimal, rather the most suitable choice depends strongly on the structure of the fluid problem, the computational objective and the constraints of the target quantum platform. The main takeaway is therefore that encoding should be assessed as an integral part of the QCFD design pipeline and revisited iteratively throughout the design pipeline, as different algorithmic components interact and influence one another.

title: Recent Advances in Privacy-Preserving Cybersecurity Using Homomorphic Encryption and Federated Learning
abstract: Cybersecurity threats and the need to secure sensitive data have grown significantly as connected devices, IoT, cloud computing, and digital services have all exploded. This review examines the most recent developments in privacy-preserving cybersecurity, with a particular emphasis on Federated Learning (FL) and Homomorphic Encryption (HE). Digital signatures, hash functions, zero-knowledge proofs, Secure Multi-party Computation, and Denial-of-Service, Malware, Phishing, SQL Injection, Session Hijacking, Man-in-the-Middle, and Cross-Site Scripting are some of the methods covered. There are three main varieties of HE covered in the study: Partial Homomorphic Encryption, Somewhat Homomorphic Encryption, and Fully Homomorphic Encryption. HE is a method for computing without decrypting the data. Additionally, FL is covered as a decentralized ML strategy that uses data retention at the local level and updates models through distribution, similar to Horizontal, Vertical, and Federated Transfer Learning. Issues with data heterogeneity, straggler effects, privacy protection, and security are also covered, along with other FL difficulties. Applications in the healthcare, financial, internet of things (IoT), edge computing, and industrial sectors are highlighted, and HE and FL are shown to provide more privacy in new areas of application as well as safer, more collaborative, and more efficient cybersecurity solutions.

title: Time-Varying Graph Convolutional Networks with Adaptive Message Passing
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various graph-based learning tasks. However, traditional GCNs operate under the assumption of a static graph structure, failing to effectively capture the inherent dynamics present in many real-world networks. This paper proposes a novel Time-Varying Graph Convolutional Network (TV-GCN) architecture that addresses this limitation by dynamically adapting its message passing parameters. The core idea is to utilize a recurrent neural network to learn and optimize the message passing rates and aggregation functions in real-time, responding to changes in the graph's topology and node importance. We introduce a mechanism for estimating node importance, using a learnable function, and then adjust the message passing rates and aggregation functions based on these importance scores. This adaptive approach allows the TV-GCN to maintain robust performance in evolving graph environments. The key contributions of this work are a flexible framework for modeling dynamic graphs and an effective method for adapting the GCN's internal parameters. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed TV-GCN compared to static GCNs in several dynamic graph scenarios.

title: Cognitive Graph Representation Learning for Commonsense Reasoning
abstract: Commonsense reasoning, the ability to draw inferences and make judgments based on implicit knowledge about the world, remains a significant challenge for artificial intelligence. Current graph representation learning (GRL) techniques often fall short due to their reliance on purely structural information, neglecting the contextual understanding and cognitive processes involved in human reasoning. This paper proposes a novel approach – Cognitive Graph Representation Learning – that integrates principles from cognitive science into the GRL framework. We introduce a method that explicitly models events, objects, and their relationships using cognitive representations, allowing the network to 'reason' about scenarios in a more human-like manner. This approach leverages concepts such as mental models, causal reasoning, and belief revision to enhance the quality of graph embeddings. The core idea is to transform the graph structure into a representation that reflects not only the connections between nodes but also the underlying cognitive processes influencing those connections. The resulting representations are then utilized for downstream commonsense reasoning tasks. We demonstrate that this method significantly improves performance compared to traditional GRL techniques, highlighting the potential of cognitive-inspired approaches for advancing commonsense reasoning in AI.

title: Program Synthesis via Constraint Satisfaction Solver Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the potential for optimizing constraint satisfaction solvers (CS solvers) to significantly enhance the efficiency and quality of program synthesis. Traditional approaches to program synthesis often focus on improving the synthesis methods themselves, while this work proposes a novel strategy centered on directly optimizing the CS solver component. The core claim is that targeted optimization of CS solvers can dramatically improve program generation. This is achieved through a two-pronged approach: firstly, employing program analysis techniques to aggressively prune the search space of the CS solver; and secondly, integrating heuristic search algorithms to refine the solver's search strategy. The research demonstrates a tangible improvement in synthesis performance compared to standard CS solver configurations. The key contributions lie in recognizing the CS solver as a critical bottleneck and providing a systematic framework for its optimization, opening new avenues for high-performance program synthesis.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Distributed Memory Access
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to distributed memory access leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core idea centers on utilizing the non-local nature of entanglement to achieve ultra-fast data retrieval over long distances without traditional data transmission. We propose a network architecture comprised of entangled quantum bits (qubits), where each node stores a portion of the total data. A measurement performed on a qubit within this network instantaneously reveals the correlated data stored in another, distant qubit. This approach circumvents the limitations of classical communication, potentially offering significant performance improvements for data access in distributed systems. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlines key challenges, and discusses future research directions. The fundamental equation driving this concept is: $E = h\nu$, where *E* represents energy, *h* is Planck's constant, and *ν* is the frequency of the emitted quantum state. We further explore the concept of entanglement through the following equation: $|\Psi\rangle = \sum_{i} \alpha_i |i\rangle \otimes |i\rangle$, representing a maximally entangled state between two qubits, where |i⟩ represents the state of each qubit. The success of this system relies heavily on maintaining the integrity of the entanglement, a factor addressed within the discussion.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Network Embedding via Optimal Transport
abstract: Bayesian Networks (BNs) are powerful tools for representing and reasoning under uncertainty. However, traditional inference methods within BNs can be computationally expensive, particularly for complex networks with numerous variables and dependencies. This paper introduces a novel approach – Dynamic Bayesian Network Embedding via Optimal Transport – to efficiently represent and manipulate BNs by embedding them into a continuous space. We utilize Optimal Transport (OT) to map nodes and edges of the BN, guided by their conditional probability distributions, into this space. The resulting embedding minimizes transport costs between related nodes, effectively capturing the network's structure. This allows for approximate inference using techniques like diffusion maps, offering a significant performance improvement over traditional BN inference methods. Our approach provides a fundamentally new way to view and process BNs, opening opportunities for dynamic modeling and reasoning. The core of this method lies in the application of OT, a technique commonly used in image processing, to the domain of Bayesian Networks, fundamentally shifting the paradigm for BN inference.

title: From Pixels to Stroma: AI-Driven Spatial Profiling of Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts on H&E and Its Implications for Immunotherapy
abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has transformed cancer therapy, but clinical responses remain heterogeneous across tumor types and patient populations. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are key stromal components of the tumor microenvironment and can contribute to immunotherapy resistance through immune exclusion, extracellular matrix remodeling, chemokine signaling, and interactions with suppressive immune cells. Although CAF-directed strategies are under active investigation, their clinical translation is limited by marked CAF heterogeneity and the lack of scalable biomarkers for patient stratification. Computational pathology based on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) provides a potential approach for extracting stromal and spatial features from routine histology, although digitized WSIs and the infrastructure required for large-scale AI analysis are not universally available. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on CAF classification, CAF-mediated immunotherapy resistance, H&E-based computational pathology, and emerging histology-based biomarker models. We further propose a conceptual roadmap for developing CAF-aware H&E spatial signatures with potential relevance to future immunotherapy stratification. Current evidence supports the biological rationale and computational feasibility of this approach, whereas its clinical utility remains to be established through rigorous external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

title: When Data Quality Outperforms Architecture: An Empirical Investigation of the Architecture-Selection Threshold in NLP Text Classification
abstract: The data-centric artificial intelligence (AI) paradigm posits that improvements to training data quality yield greater performance increases compared to changes to model architecture; however, the claim is currently supported by case studies and demonstrations rather than controlled experiments. The experiments used five corpora with varying amounts of label noise (0.0% to 54.7%) and three distinct model architectures (LinearSVC, DistilBERT, and RoBERTa), resulting in 135 total experimental conditions based on the combination of two remediation strategies applied across five thresholds. All conditions were assessed via five-fold stratified cross-validation. Label errors within the five corpora were identified using confident learning (a probabilistic approach to flagging potentially mislabeled training examples by comparing predicted class probabilities with observed labels). The identification of label errors were validated independently against the CIFAR-N benchmark prior to conducting downstream analyses. To aid in connecting the results of this research to practice, cost-performance Pareto frontiers were created for each of four distinct levels of annotation costs. Lastly, a theoretical framework was developed to explain the observed architecture-noise interaction patterns.

title: High-Dimensional Clustering Methods
abstract: High-dimensional clustering presents unique challenges in modern data analysis, particularly in HDLSS settings. This chapter provides a comprehensive treatment of clustering methodologies for high-dimensional data, encompassing hierarchical, partitioning, density-based, and change point-based approaches. We introduce a novel proximity-based clustering method, the Change Point Clustering (CPC) algorithm, which leverages dissimilarity measures and distance concentration phenomena to construct clusters with theoretical guarantees of consistency as the dimension grows. The CPC method utilizes the distance difference matrix and an agreement matrix based on the Rand index to determine optimal cluster boundaries, effectively reducing the https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> N × d data matrix to an https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> N × N matrix for computational efficiency. Comparative studies against https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> k M ρ , HDBSCAN, and MST demonstrate superior performance in various high-dimensional distributions. The chapter also discusses strategies for estimating the number of clusters, the influence of distance metrics, and the limitations posed by correlated variables on distance concentration. Applications to real datasets, including Lymphoma data, illustrate practical utility, providing guidance for high-dimensional clustering in genomics, finance, and other complex domains.

title: XAI in Model Training
abstract: In general, the XAI methods are applied as post-hoc in DL models to get the explanations on the decisions generated by the models. However, if the XAI methods are integrated during the training phase of the DL models, they will support the early detection of bias, overfitting, and correlation errors. In addition, it helps in the validation of learning done by the model based on feature importance. This will lead to efficient debugging of the model and error correction in the faulty representations. This refined approach transforms the black-box training nature of the DL models into a transparent, interpretable, and auditable workflow of the DL model. This chapter discusses some of the potential ways to integrate XAI methods during training so that a paradigm shift will be achieved in the black-box nature of DL model training.

title: Integrating XAI in Agentic AI Architecture
abstract: The current advancement of AI in Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled the development of multi-agent systems to solve complex applications in real-time domains such as healthcare, finance, and industrial applications. To achieve this, each individual agent performs a functionality or module in the application. For instance, in a healthcare application, the agents can be designed to automate tasks such as diagnosis, treatment planning, patient monitoring, along with administrative activities regarding patient records management. In such a set-up, each agent operates autonomously and at the same time collaborates with other agents to achieve the global goal. Such a framework is termed an “Agentic AI System” that helps in providing better solutions to complex problem domains with reduced complexity. However, the internal working of each of these agents is a black box and hence they need to be explained so that the trustworthiness of their functionalities can be achieved. Hence, this chapter provides a detailed study on how Explainable AI (XAI) provides the explanations on such internal workings so that the stakeholders can understand the functionality of the entire system, which thus leads to the trustworthiness of the system.

title: An Improved Attraction-Repulsion OptimizationAlgorithm for Global Optimization and EngineeringDesign Problems
abstract: Attraction-Repulsion Optimization Algorithm (AROA) is a recently proposed meta-heuristic algorithm known for its simplicity, ease of implementation, and robustness. However, AROA may converge to local optima when applied to complex optimization problems. To address this limitation, we propose an enhanced version called the Differential Cauchy Tangent Attraction-Repulsion Optimization Algorithm (DCTAROA). First, we propose a mutation operator based on a tangent flight mutation strategy and a dimension decision mechanism using the inverse cumulative distribution function of the Cauchy distribution. The tangent flight mutation enhances the local search capability and accelerates convergence, while the dimension decision strategy of the Cauchy distribution inverse cumulative function increases population diversity and improves exploration efficiency. Subsequently, we integrate Differential Evolution (DE) as a local search mechanism to strengthen the global optimization performance of AROA. To evaluate the proposed algorithm, we compare it with 15 state-of-the-art algorithms on 29 CEC2017 benchmark functions across various dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate that DCTAROA outperforms the compared algorithms in terms of solution accuracy, stability, convergence speed, and statistical significance based on the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Furthermore, we apply DCTAROAto three practical engineering design problems. The results confirm that DCTAROA effectively explores the search space and yields competitive solutions, thereby validating its practical applicability.
