title: Методы и алгоритмы поддержки принятия решений при управлении выбором участков бурения в геологоразведочных работах на основе тензорного анализа
abstract: This paper presents a new approach to decision support in geological exploration management based on tensor analysis methods. A management concept has been developed that integrates tensor calculus methods with organizational decision-making cycles and accounts for current geomagnetic conditions when establishing priorities for the objective function. A tensor model of the geophysical field featuring an adaptive metric tensor is proposed, ensuring the preservation of the structural integrity of multi-component data. A visualization method based on super-ellipsoidal glyphs and adaptive clustering has been created. A research prototype of a web application was developed and demonstrated superiority over commercial counterparts: data processing speed increased by 8–24 percent, deposit boundary detection accuracy reached an F1-score of 0.82, visual analysis time was reduced by 30 percent, and positioning error decreased by 25–30 percent. The results demonstrate the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency of geological exploration by comprehensively accounting for the tensor nature of geophysical data.

title: Consequence-Preserving Projections: Semantic Assurance for Agent Tool Interfaces
abstract: Consequence-Preserving Projections is carrier-neutral research software for Projection Assurance: checking whether consequence-relevant semantics survive projection into agent-facing interfaces. Version 0.7.0 separates a Source Consequence Contract from a hash-pinned Projection Adapter, generates the complete declared finite realization domain and source consequence map from contract rules, keeps target semantic compilation consequence-blind, and issues proof-carrying certificates that can be checked through a compact consumer path independent of the producer verifier/compiler stack. The release includes canonical GitHub and Azure projections, carrier-neutral examples, cross-runtime qualification, adversarial and metamorphic checks, cryptographic provenance, and one-command offline reproduction. Results are model-relative; live-runtime conformance and independent reproduction are not claimed.

title: The Quantum Pi Benchmark: Superposed-Address BBP Computation and Bounded Search Primitives
abstract: The Quantum Pi Benchmark separates oracle-construction provenance (P0–P4), controller blindness (B0 or B1), and a non-total capability grid (R). Quantum search over digit patterns requires an oracle that preserves an address superposition while computing address-dependent data. This paper describes testing of that requirement for low hexadecimal digits of Pi using Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe (BBP)-derived reversible arithmetic on IBM Heron r2 QPU, Kingston. Two direct multiplexed constructions fail at 738–1038 routed native CZ gates despite exact noiseless validation. A prefix compute–uncompute echo localizes a selected implementation’s collapse to the second multiplexed stage. Reachable-cone synthesis restricts exactness to declared protected trajectories and reduces the core to 47 routed native CZ gates. Across eighteen runs, per-branch digit success is 0.69–0.84, cross-pair support remains below 0.02, and roundtrip return is 0.56–0.74; these jointly support a preserved address-conditioned structure, while the correlation gap alone is not a coherence proof. A P0/B0/R2 compiled Grover layer amplifies Pi-table offsets: sixteen-candidate bands return the mark at 0.618–0.688, and ten 64-candidate single-iteration runs return it at 2.2–2.9 times the uniform reference. A separate 34-decision outer loop correctly classifies occupied versus empty tiles, but fails its original earliest-position objective, and is therefore reported as tile-occurrence classification. At a fixed four-position tile, one declared comparator consumes a BBP-computed digit; target rotation and Ramsey controls support P3/B0/R5. The final thirteen-tile campaign uses execution-locked BBP bodies and target-independent phase calibration, however, known codewords select or omit its discriminator and only planner-positive tiles receive confirmation. The final campaign supports a bounded P4/B0/R6 range validation.

title: Predictive Decision States (PDS): Reproducibility Package
abstract: This reproducibility package accompanies the study on Predictive Decision States (PDS) for multiscale knowledge auditing of trained visual classifiers. The archive contains the study-specific analysis code, dataset and split manifests, precomputed image embeddings, frozen model artifacts, expert-informed registry files, trained analysis artifacts, result tables, and supplementary material required to reproduce the computational analyses reported in the study. The workflow covers predictive-response extraction, fixed-probe evaluation, construction and comparison of multiscale decision-state hierarchies, external knowledge auditing, robustness and control analyses, and multiscale relational trajectory analysis. The study evaluates four visual backbones—DenseNet121, EfficientNet-Lite0, ConvNeXt V2-Nano, and DINOv2 ViT-S/14—on a 120-species citizen-science fungal image dataset. The expert-informed visual-ambiguity registry is used only as an independently specified external audit layer and does not affect PDS construction or relation selection. Original source photographs are not redistributed in this archive and remain subject to the licensing and availability terms of their source platform. The included manifests preserve the information required to reconstruct the study dataset where source images remain available. For implementation details, archive structure, computational requirements, and the reproducibility workflow, see the included README and Supplementary Material.

title: ScatterWorks
abstract: ScatterWorks scatterworks is a Python package for building and solving scattering-networkmodels. It keeps the directed network geometry separate from the localscattering matrices, then assembles them into global operators for spectra,transport, and finite-device calculations. The same network object can represent periodic unit cells and finite systems.Its explicit link basis makes local scattering templates and the flow of waveamplitudes straightforward to inspect. Installation ScatterWorks requires Python 3.11 or newer. Install the core package with: pip install scatterworks Install the optional Bokeh plotting support with: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[plot]"``` Install symbolic scattering support with: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[symbolic]"``` Install the optional MUMPS-backed sparse solver with: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[solver]"``` Optional features can be installed together. For example, to install allthree extras, run: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[plot,symbolic,solver]"``` For an editable source checkout, run `pip install -e .`. The repository uses[Pixi](https://pixi.sh/) for development. Build the documentationfrom the repository root with: ```bashpixi run docs-build``` Quick start A network is defined by integer rows containing a source node and a sink node: import numpy as npimport scatterworks as sw links = np.array( [ [0, 1], [1, 0], ], dtype=int,) network = sw.Network(links)print(network.links) For a periodic model, append one integer unit-cell shift per lattice dimensionto each row: unit_cell_links = np.array( [ [0, 1, 0, 0], [0, 1, -1, -1], [1, 0, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0, 1], ], dtype=int,) unit_cell = sw.Network(unit_cell_links) After defining the topology, usescatterworks.scattering.scattering_equations to assemble local scatteringmatrices into a global operator. Lead-to-lead problems can be solved with`scatterworks.scattering.solve_scattering_equations` or`scatterworks.scattering.schur_solve`. Documentation - Start with the [network model basics](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/basics.md).- Work through the [Fabry-Perot interferometer](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/fabry_perot_interferometer.md) for a small finite example.- See the [Chalker-Coddington network](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/chalker_coddington.md) for a periodic unit cell.- Follow the [Kagome ribbon tutorial](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/relink_kagome.md) to cut and relink a finite strip.- Browse the [package reference](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/packagereference.md) for the Python API. Zenodo archive scatterworks/ contains the package source and tests. publication/ and docs/ contain the manuscript sources, figures, and tutorials. pyproject.toml and pixi.lock define the reproducible environment; standalone examples and the arXiv-only minted cache are excluded. Paper simulations paper_simulations/ contains the scripts used to generate the manuscript figures. The included conductance dataset reproduces the published plots without rerunning the full cluster calculation. Run figure scripts from paper_simulations/; generated figures are written to publication/figures/.

evidence.abstract: ScatterWorks scatterworks is a Python package for building and solving scattering-networkmodels. It keeps the directed network geometry separate from the localscattering matrices, then assembles them into global operators for spectra,transport, and finite-device calculations. The same network object can represent periodic unit cells and finite systems.Its explicit link basis makes local scattering templates and the flow of waveamplitudes straightforward to inspect. Installation ScatterWorks requires Python 3.11 or newer. Install the core package with: pip install scatterworks Install the optional Bokeh plotting support with: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[plot]"``` Install symbolic scattering support with: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[symbolic]"``` Install the optional MUMPS-backed sparse solver with: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[solver]"``` Optional features can be installed together. For example, to install allthree extras, run: ```bashpip install "scatterworks[plot,symbolic,solver]"``` For an editable source checkout, run `pip install -e .`. The repository uses[Pixi](https://pixi.sh/) for development. Build the documentationfrom the repository root with: ```bashpixi run docs-build``` Quick start A network is defined by integer rows containing a source node and a sink node: import numpy as npimport scatterworks as sw links = np.array( [ [0, 1], [1, 0], ], dtype=int,) network = sw.Network(links)print(network.links) For a periodic model, append one integer unit-cell shift per lattice dimensionto each row: unit_cell_links = np.array( [ [0, 1, 0, 0], [0, 1, -1, -1], [1, 0, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0, 1], ], dtype=int,) unit_cell = sw.Network(unit_cell_links) After defining the topology, usescatterworks.scattering.scattering_equations to assemble local scatteringmatrices into a global operator. Lead-to-lead problems can be solved with`scatterworks.scattering.solve_scattering_equations` or`scatterworks.scattering.schur_solve`. Documentation - Start with the [network model basics](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/basics.md).- Work through the [Fabry-Perot interferometer](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/fabry_perot_interferometer.md) for a small finite example.- See the [Chalker-Coddington network](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/chalker_coddington.md) for a periodic unit cell.- Follow the [Kagome ribbon tutorial](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/relink_kagome.md) to cut and relink a finite strip.- Browse the [package reference](https://gitlab.kwant-project.org/qt/scatterworks/-/blob/main/docs/source/packagereference.md) for the Python API. Zenodo archive scatterworks/ contains the package source and tests. publication/ and docs/ contain the manuscript sources, figures, and tutorials. pyproject.toml and pixi.lock define the reproducible environment; standalone examples and the arXiv-only minted cache are excluded. Paper simulations paper_simulations/ contains the scripts used to generate the manuscript figures. The included conductance dataset reproduces the published plots without rerunning the full cluster calculation. Run figure scripts from paper_simulations/; generated figures are written to publication/figures/.

title: Certified Robustness of Deep Learning Models via Abstract Interpretation
abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various domains, but their vulnerability to adversarial attacks and sensitivity to noisy inputs pose significant challenges. Traditional methods for evaluating model robustness rely on empirical testing, which can be unreliable and provide limited guarantees. This paper proposes a novel approach to certified robustness of deep learning models by leveraging abstract interpretation techniques. We demonstrate how abstract interpretation can provide rigorous guarantees about the model's behavior under input perturbations. The core idea is to apply abstract interpretation methods to the computational graph of a deep learning model to derive abstract bounds on the model's output for different input perturbations. These bounds represent a formal guarantee of robustness, allowing us to quantify the model's resilience to adversarial attacks and noisy data. This work offers a formal and verifiable method for ensuring the robustness of deep learning models, addressing a critical gap in the field.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing for Quantum State Tomography
abstract: Quantum state tomography (QST) is a fundamental technique for characterizing quantum systems, but it often suffers from significant experimental challenges, including high measurement complexity and resource demands. This paper explores the potential of hyperdimensional computing (HDC) as a viable alternative to traditional QST. HDC leverages high-dimensional vectors to represent and manipulate quantum states, allowing for the development of algorithms that exploit inherent correlations to reconstruct quantum state information with reduced measurement requirements. The core claim is that HDC offers a potentially efficient and scalable approach to QST. This work details the theoretical framework, outlining key algorithms and highlighting the advantages of utilizing HDC for quantum state characterization. The focus is on demonstrating the feasibility of this approach through conceptual design, emphasizing the reduced complexity compared to conventional QST methods. We propose a framework for representing quantum states within HDC vectors and present a simplified reconstruction algorithm.

title: Quantum-Inspired Cryptographic Key Exchange with Entangled State Verification
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cryptographic key exchange protocol inspired by quantum mechanics, specifically leveraging the principles of entanglement to enhance security against eavesdropping attacks. Traditional classical key exchange protocols, such as Diffie-Hellman, are susceptible to compromise due to the inherent vulnerabilities in mathematical computations and key distribution. Our approach introduces a verification step based on a measurement of an entangled state, providing a fundamentally different security model. The shared key is derived from the outcome of this measurement, and any attempt to intercept or manipulate the entangled state during transmission will inevitably introduce detectable errors, thus alerting the legitimate parties. We formalize the protocol with mathematical equations, outlining the key generation process and the eavesdropping detection mechanism. The core of the system relies on the uncertainty principle and the correlated nature of entangled states. This system presents a potential pathway towards more robust key exchange mechanisms, particularly as classical cryptography faces increasing pressure from advancements in computational power. The protocol's security is directly tied to the difficulty of accurately replicating the entangled state and performing the required measurement, offering a defense against sophisticated attacks.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Hybrid Models for Causal Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to neuro-symbolic hybrid models, integrating neural networks with symbolic logic and, crucially, incorporating a causal reasoning engine. The core challenge in neuro-symbolic systems lies in effectively bridging the gap between data-driven learning and explicit knowledge representation, particularly in the realm of causal inference. Existing approaches often struggle to provide robust explanations and reliable predictions, especially when dealing with complex, high-dimensional systems. Our proposed framework addresses this limitation by leveraging causal graphs to model relationships between variables, thereby enabling deeper understanding and improved predictive accuracy. The neural network component handles the learning from raw data, while the symbolic logic component provides the structural knowledge and logical reasoning capabilities. The causal reasoning engine, built upon the causal graph, facilitates multi-level inference and allows for the identification of crucial causal pathways. We detail the architecture, the integration strategy, and the theoretical underpinnings of this system, demonstrating its potential for applications in domains requiring both accurate predictions and interpretable explanations, such as medical diagnosis, financial modeling, and robotics. The key contribution is the enhancement of causal reasoning within neuro-symbolic models, leading to increased model interpretability and trustworthiness. The proposed system aims to move beyond simple correlation detection to truly understanding cause-and-effect relationships.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Multi-Agent Systems with Emergent Behavior
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to modeling multi-agent systems exhibiting emergent behavior, leveraging the power of probabilistic programming. Traditional methods struggle to capture the intricate dynamics of these systems due to combinatorial explosion and the difficulty in representing uncertainty. We argue that probabilistic programming offers a fundamentally better paradigm by allowing agents' behaviors to be defined as stochastic processes. This approach facilitates continuous, probabilistic exploration of agent interactions, leading to the natural emergence of collective patterns. The core of this work is the formalization of multi-agent systems using probabilistic models, enabling the simulation of complex interactions and providing a framework for analyzing and understanding emergent phenomena. We outline the key components of this framework, including the representation of agent states, actions, and interactions, along with the probabilistic inference techniques used to analyze the resulting simulations. The presented methodology offers a significant advancement in modeling complex systems where emergent behavior is a defining characteristic.

title: Hybrid Offline-Online Multi-Agent Decision Transformers for Wireless Resource Management
abstract: This paper develops a hybrid offline-online multi-agent reinforcement learning framework based on decision transformers. The policy is first pretrained offline via supervised sequence modeling of trajectories generated by existing policies, providing a safe and sample-efficient initialization. It is then fine-tuned online using a hybrid objective that incorporates critic-guided gradients, enabling performance improvements beyond the offline policy. To facilitate stable offline-to-online transfer and effective multi-agent coordination, the framework incorporates return-weighted sampling, a critic conditioned on neighbors' actions, and neighborhood-correlated exploration. The approach is fully distributed: both training and execution rely only on local observations and limited information exchange among neighboring agents. Evaluations with dynamic traffic arrivals in two settings: (i) joint scheduling and power allocation and (ii) coordinated beamforming, show that the proposed method achieves quality-of-service (QoS) performance comparable to centralized methods. Moreover, when pretrained on lower-quality datasets, online fine-tuning is also observed to surpass the initial offline policy. These results demonstrate a promising learning-based alternative for wireless resource management.

title: Lossy Event Compression: From Event Stream Distortion to Task Performance
abstract: Event cameras generate asynchronous, sparse data streams with microsecond temporal resolution, but in moderate-to-high motion scenes they can produce as many as hundreds of millions of events per second, creating significant bandwidth and storage challenges. Lossy compression is therefore essential for practical deployment, yet existing event stream distortion metrics fail to reliably predict compression-induced degradation at the task level, forcing codec optimization to rely on expensive task-specific evaluations. To address this gap, this paper introduces two fundamentally different event compression pipelines: i) an aggregation-based pipeline that converts the event stream into polarity-based histogram frames for compression with the conventional image codec JPEG 2000, and ii) a frame-free point cloud-based pipeline that codes events natively as 3D points using the octree-based codec G-PCC. Both pipelines are then assessed within a unified task-driven evaluation framework that relates event stream distortion to downstream application performance across four representative tasks: i) video reconstruction, ii) object detection, iii) optical flow estimation, and a delay-sensitive task iv) asynchronous feature tracking under a reference-relative protocol. Building on this framework, five classification-based distortion metrics are applied to event compression for the first time, to the best of the authors' knowledge, and benchmarked against existing event stream metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed metrics reliably predict compression-induced task degradation across different coding frameworks. This demonstrates that event stream distortion assessment can be an efficient alternative to repeated task-specific evaluation, providing direct guidance for the development and optimization of future event data coding solutions.

title: Beyond Pairwise Graphs in Science: Hypergraph Adaptive Wavelet Operators for Parametric PDEs
abstract: Physical systems are often modeled by solution operators that map input fields, parameters, geometries, or past states to steady or future physical states. Learning these maps is difficult, especially for time-dependent systems that must assimilate history and remain stable under autoregressive rollout. Many neural operators work best on regular, structured grids, while realistic simulations often require unstructured meshes or point clouds to resolve complex geometries; in such settings, grid-centric representations can lose accuracy. Graph neural operators handle these domains through message passing or spectral graph filtering, but pairwise edges do not directly capture group-wise couplings among mesh cells, local neighborhoods, or conservation volumes. We introduce the Hypergraph Adaptive waveLet Operator (HALO), which lifts the domain to a hypergraph and learns in its spectral wavelet domain. HALO avoids explicit hypergraph-Laplacian eigendecomposition through Chebyshev polynomial wavelet filters, giving localized spectral kernels at linear sparse-matrix cost. Its trainable dyadic wavelet scales are regularized toward tight-frame coverage, allowing the frequency response to adapt to each PDE while encouraging stable multi-scale spectral coverage. Across 2D and 3D benchmarks on structured and unstructured discretizations, HALO achieves best or near-best accuracy among frequency-, transformer-, DeepONet-, state-space-, and graph-based baselines and sustains stable multi-step rollouts. The same model scales to industrial aerodynamic geometries: on meshes of a few hundred thousand points it is on par with, or better than, the strongest fixed-discretization transformers, while remaining resolution-equivariant.

title: Guardrail Verdicts Are Not Serialization-Invariant, Replication Artifact
abstract: Data and code to reproduce the results in "Guardrail Verdicts Are Not Serialization-Invariant: Prompt-Format Sensitivity of Safety Guardrails Near the Decision Boundary for LLM Agents" (Leburu, Gupta, Vallabhaneni; IEEE Access, 2026). A pre-specified measurement study of whether deployed LLM-agent safety guardrails return the same block/allow verdict when a tool call is re-serialized in ways no JSON parser distinguishes (indentation, key order, whitespace). Across five decision-capable guardrails from three independent vendor lineages (Meta Llama Guard 3, IBM Granite Guardian, Alibaba Qwen3Guard), every guard flips its verdict on a substantial fraction of the actions it blocks (per-guard 19–50%, pooled 35%). Includes the frozen 146-task grid with its pre-specified content hash, the expanded grid, pinned model digests, the pre-specification document, and the complete verdict logs.

title: Enterprise AI Success: Definition Before Development
abstract: Most enterprise AI initiatives stumble not because of poor models, but because teams skip the critical step of defining what success actually looks like. Without clear business outcomes first, even production-ready ML systems deliver no value. Full article: https://davidohnstad.net/enterprise-ai-success-definition-before-development/

title: Exact conditioned-target exclusions for a binary Legendre pair of length 115 via shared column frontiers
abstract: Length 115 is the smallest length for which the existence of a binary Legendre pair is unresolved. We describe an exact, certificate-producing computational method that operates inside the fixed-marginal 5x23 formulation of the problem. For a fixed margin instance, a packed column-by-column frontier computes, without approximation, the complete attainable set of joint periodic-autocorrelation signatures at shifts 5, 10, and 23; the Legendre condition then admits exactly 6,155 compatible signature pairs ("conditioned targets"). A split meet-in-the-middle continuation decides, for a chosen target, the exact achievable shift-15 values on each side, and, when needed, the exact shift-20 values on every surviving branch. An empty complement join is an exact exclusion of that conditioned target. A shared-frontier refinement batches targets that agree in their first two signature coordinates and carries the third coordinate as a relation payload; in its largest campaign this reduced the required root workload by 85.1% relative to independent per-target runs. Using this machinery, 29 occupancy-ranked conditioned targets (ranks 1-22, 29, 36, 37, 42, 45, 46, and 60) are exactly excluded, with cross-host reproduction, an immutable regression oracle, and SHA-256-manifested certificates. We state the claim boundary precisely: these exclusions concern individual conditioned targets within one margin instance; they do not exclude the margin instance, any multiplier class, or length 115. The first 100 occupancy ranks cover only 0.0073% of the compatible terminal-pair mass, so the value of the work lies in the method, the reusable exact machinery, and the certificate corpus (which we propose as regression oracles for future implementations) rather than in progress toward a nonexistence proof. The supplementary archive contains all 29 machine-checkable exclusion certificates, the campaign-level manifests and audits, four durable campaign summaries, a machine-readable SHA-256 source map, and the canonical margin-instance input file.

title: Adversarial Learning for Program Security
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adversarial learning techniques to enhance program security against malicious attacks and data corruption. Traditional security approaches often rely on static defenses that are vulnerable to adaptive adversaries. Adversarial learning offers a dynamic solution by training models to recognize and mitigate adversarial examples – inputs specifically crafted to mislead a program. This work presents a framework for incorporating adversarial learning into program security, focusing on the core claim that training models to identify adversarial samples and using those samples for training can significantly improve program robustness. The proposed methodology addresses the emerging threat of adversarial attacks, aiming to create more resilient and reliable software systems. This paper outlines the core mechanism, detailing the training process and the resulting improvements in a program's ability to withstand interference. The evaluation focuses on the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating its potential to provide a novel and robust defense strategy. ---

title: LargeRDFBench Interoperable Edition: RDF Datasets, HDT Indexes, Queries and Expected Results
abstract: LargeRDFBench Interoperable Edition A drop-in replacement for the data and expected results of LargeRDFBench, the billion-triple benchmark for SPARQL endpoint federation (Saleem et al., Journal of Web Semantics, 2018). Several of the original data dumps violate the RDF specifications, so engines with strict parsers cannot load them, and the expected results ship in an ad hoc format. This edition repairs both. The benchmark itself is unchanged: no triple is added or removed, no query is rewritten — only malformed terms are corrected and serialisations normalised. Triple counts per dataset are preserved, so results obtained here stay comparable to results reported against the original. Contents Data: 13 datasets, 1,003,960,176 triples, as valid UTF-8 N-Triples, with HDT counterparts. Queries: the full suite of 40: S1–S14 (simple), C1–C10 (complex), L1–L8 (large data), CH1–CH8 (complex + large data). Expected results: W3C SPARQL 1.1 Query Results JSON Format, with encoding defects fixed throughout and the result sets for S7, C7 and C8 corrected against the source data. What changed Malformed IRIs, literals and language tags rewritten to conform to RDF 1.1; all dumps re-serialised as valid UTF-8 N-Triples. Expected results converted from the original ad hoc format to SPARQL 1.1 Query Results JSON. Three result sets (S7, C7, C8) recomputed against the repaired data. Provenance Modernisation pipeline: Result validation: Original benchmark: Raw source dumps: Citation Please cite the original benchmark alongside this edition. Saleem, M., Hasnain, A., & Ngonga Ngomo, A.-C. (2018). LargeRDFBench: A billion triples benchmark for SPARQL endpoint federation. Journal of Web Semantics, 48, 85–125. Tam, B.-E., Saleem, M., & Taelman, R. (2026). Strengthening LargeRDFBench for Interoperable Federated SPARQL Evaluation. DMKG 2026, co-located with ISWC 2026, Bari, Italy. CEUR Workshop Proceedings. The benchmark itself is unchanged: no triple is added or removed, no query is rewritten — only malformed terms are corrected and serialisations normalised. Triple counts per dataset are preserved, so results obtained here stay comparable to results reported against the original. Contents Data: 13 datasets, 1,003,960,176 triples, as valid UTF-8 N-Triples, with HDT counterparts. Queries: the full suite of 40: S1–S14 (simple), C1–C10 (complex), L1–L8 (large data), CH1–CH8 (complex + large data). Expected results: W3C SPARQL 1.1 Query Results JSON Format, with encoding defects fixed throughout and the result sets for S7, C7 and C8 corrected against the source data. What changed Malformed IRIs, literals and language tags rewritten to conform to RDF 1.1; all dumps re-serialised as valid UTF-8 N-Triples. Expected results converted from the original ad hoc format to SPARQL 1.1 Query Results JSON. Three result sets (S7, C7, C8) recomputed against the repaired data. Provenance Modernisation pipeline: Result validation: Original benchmark: Raw source dumps: Citation Please cite the original benchmark alongside this edition. Saleem, M., Hasnain, A., & Ngonga Ngomo, A.-C. (2018). LargeRDFBench: A billion triples benchmark for SPARQL endpoint federation. Journal of Web Semantics, 48, 85–125. Tam, B.-E., Saleem, M., & Taelman, R. (2026). Strengthening LargeRDFBench for Interoperable Federated SPARQL Evaluation. DMKG 2026, co-located with ISWC 2026, Bari, Italy. CEUR Workshop Proceedings. title: Hierarchical Information Bottleneck with Dynamic Compression
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to representation learning called Hierarchical Information Bottleneck with Dynamic Compression. The core idea is to construct a hierarchical architecture where information is progressively filtered at different levels of abstraction. This is achieved by employing multiple bottleneck layers, each with dynamically adjustable compression rates. These rates adapt based on the current level of abstraction and the relevance of information, facilitated by a feedback loop between levels. The system learns representations that are both informative and concise, leading to a more robust and efficient learning process compared to traditional methods. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and their interactions. The system's architecture offers a flexible and adaptable solution for a variety of representation learning tasks.

title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Deep Neural Network Representations
abstract: This paper investigates the representational capacity of deep neural networks from an information-theoretic perspective. Traditional evaluations of deep learning models often focus on accuracy and performance metrics, neglecting the fundamental question of how efficiently these networks encode information. We introduce a framework utilizing mutual information, entropy, and related measures to quantify the information content within the hidden layers of deep neural networks. Our analysis reveals that the representations learned by these networks may not be optimally compressed, suggesting potential redundancy and avenues for improving model design and training strategies. The core claim is that deep neural networks learn representations that are not necessarily efficient in terms of information compression. This work contributes a rigorous, quantitative method for understanding and potentially optimizing deep neural network representations, moving beyond purely empirical observations.

title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Neural Network Representations
abstract: This paper investigates the analysis of neural network representations using information-theoretic principles. Traditional approaches to understanding these representations primarily rely on empirical observations and visualization techniques, often lacking a rigorous mathematical foundation. This work proposes a framework for quantifying the information content and redundancy within learned representations by employing measures such as mutual information, transfer entropy, and related concepts. The core of the analysis involves calculating these measures across different layers of a trained neural network, aiming to characterize the flow of information and identify salient features that contribute to the network's functionality. The research provides a mathematically grounded approach to neural network representation analysis, offering a more objective and quantifiable understanding compared to current subjective interpretations. The results will demonstrate how information-theoretic measures can reveal underlying structure and dependencies within representations, potentially informing the design and optimization of neural networks.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Counterfactual Reasoning in Complex Systems
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning, the ability to reason about "what if" scenarios and their potential consequences, is a fundamental cognitive process and a critical tool for decision-making in complex systems. However, the inherent complexity of these systems—characterized by intricate causal relationships, feedback loops, and uncertainty—significantly challenges traditional approaches to counterfactual analysis. This paper proposes a novel framework utilizing probabilistic programming to address these challenges. We introduce a language that allows users to explicitly model causal relationships, integrate observational data, and efficiently compute counterfactual probabilities through Bayesian inference. The core of the approach lies in the formalization of counterfactual reasoning within a probabilistic framework, enabling rigorous analysis and prediction in scenarios where traditional methods fall short. This work demonstrates the potential of probabilistic programming to provide a robust and scalable solution for counterfactual reasoning in complex systems.

title: Euclidean Fourier Neural Operators
abstract: Fourier neural operators (FNOs) provide an efficient framework for learning mappings between function spaces as they are, by construction, independent of the grid resolution at which they are trained and evaluated. However, FNOs are not independent of the periodic domain they are applied to: their discrete spectral weights are indexed by integer Fourier mode numbers, which correspond to physical wavevectors. When applied to a different domain, the same trained weights act at different wavevectors, and the FNO silently represents a different operator. This makes FNOs unsuitable for tasks where transfer across domains is crucial. We propose Euclidean Fourier neural operators~(EFNOs) as a domain-independent alternative to FNOs. By parameterizing the spectral kernel as a continuous function of the physical wavevector, the EFNO can learn operators that act consistently across periodic domains of varying shape and size. We evaluate the EFNO on a simple heat equation and on a practically relevant materials science task of learning exchange-correlation potentials across different crystal structures, and demonstrate that the EFNO is able to generalize to unseen grid sizes and domains.

title: Post-Edit Re-Verification in Simulator-Backed Engineering Agents: A Controlled Comparison of Verification-Cadence Guidance
abstract: Engineering agents that interact with external simulators may need to coordinate design modification with reacquisition of engineering evidence for the modified state. We ask whether first post-edit re-verification changes when explicit verification-cadence guidance is retained versus omitted while verification-relevant state/facts are held constant. Cadence-Guided (CG) retained an instruction to request a new simulation after a substantive modification, whereas Cadence-Omitted (CO) removed that instruction; neither condition used a hard gate. The study therefore measures instruction-conditioned post-edit verification-policy adherence rather than spontaneous recognition that prior evidence has become stale. Using DWSIM as the simulator backend and continuous valve-pressure adjustment, five Alibaba/Qwen models were evaluated on eight synthetic cases; each model-case-condition combination was executed three times via live API calls, yielding 120 evaluation slots per condition. Re-verification was observed in 94/120 CG slots versus 32/120 CO slots; cadence violations occurred in 26/120 versus 87/120; and bounded final success was reached in 95/120 versus 35/120. qwen3.5-35b-a3b showed minimal re-verification (1/24 in CG and 0/24 in CO) and no final success in either condition. Within this bounded protocol, explicit post-edit verification-cadence guidance was associated with more re-verification, fewer cadence violations, and more frequent bounded final success, supporting the treatment of verification cadence as an explicit interaction-protocol component.

title: Modular verification of liveness properties in higher-order concurrent languages
abstract: Concurrent software is central to modern computing, powering systems such as operat- ing systems, databases, and distributed applications. Ensuring its correctness is crucial, yet inherently difficult due to unpredictable interactions between concurrently execut- ing threads. Among correctness guarantees, liveness properties—such as termination or non-blocking progress—are particularly challenging. Unlike safety properties, which deal with finite execution prefixes and can be tested for, liveness properties concern potentially infinite behaviors and therefore require a different approach. Formal verification provides a way to establish such guarantees by modeling programs mathematically and reasoning about all their possible executions. How- ever, verifying liveness properties of concurrent programs faces a major challenge of modularity. Ideally, one verifies complex programs by separately verifying their indi- vidual components and composing the results. While this is well-developed for safety, achieving similar modularity for liveness is difficult due to complex dependencies between components and their environment, including the scheduler. Capturing these dependencies in reusable specifications has been a non-trivial task. Moreover, the reasoning methods used in verifying safety of higher-order programs are not directly applicable to verifying liveness. This thesis proposes a solution for modular verification of liveness properties in higher-order concurrent languages. The approach combines two key ideas. First, it builds on a refinement-based Trillium framework which enables reasoning about live- ness in a higher-order setting. Second, it incorporates the abstractions of obligations (inspired by Sassy) to specify and verify liveness behavior compositionally. Together, these techniques yield the Lawyer program logic that supports modular reasoning about liveness, in a way analogous to established approaches for safety. The entire development is mechanized in the Rocq proof assistant on top of the Iris framework, ensuring a high degree of trust in the results. I use the Lawyer logic for verifying two kinds of properties. First, I establish termination of closed programs under different scheduling assumptions. Second, I show that certain specifications imply wait-freedom of individual operations, even in unknown higher-order contexts. Thus, the thesis established by this work is: Refinement-based program logic, combined with obligations-based reasoning, allows one to modularly verify live- ness properties of blocking and non-blocking higher-order concurrent programs.

title: CERCETARE ASUPRA IMPACTULUI ADUS ASUPRA ÎMBUNĂTĂȚIRII EXPERIENȚEI CLIENȚILOR ȘI CREȘTERII SATISFACȚIEI PRIN UTILIZAREA UNUI AGENT VIRTUAL: O ANALIZĂ A PERCEPȚIILOR ȘI COMPORTAMENTELOR CLIENȚILOR
abstract: Studiul evaluează impactul introducerii unui agent virtual conversațional bazat pe inteligență artificială asupra experienței și satisfacției clienților unei firme românești de consultanță în afaceri și management. Agentul preia interacțiunile repetitive — întrebări frecvente, stadiul solicitărilor, programări, informații despre servicii — oferind răspuns imediat și disponibilitate permanentă, și escaladează către consultantul uman doar cazurile complexe. Contextul îl constituie o firmă cu personal restrâns și portofoliu de clienți în creștere accelerată, unde interacțiunile de rutină consumă timp expert și generează întârzieri în afara programului de lucru. Cercetarea se concentrează pe percepțiile și comportamentele clienților: cum evaluează calitatea interacțiunii, în ce măsură cresc satisfacția și loialitatea, ce factori determină acceptarea tehnologiei. Designul este mixt, combinând chestionare de satisfacție (CSAT) și de recomandare (NPS), interviuri în profunzime, analiza conversațiilor cu consimțământ și o comparație între interacțiunea cu agentul virtual și cea cu un consultant uman, alături de analiza datelor financiare 2021–2025. Modelul de calcul proiectează o reducere a timpului de primă reacție de la circa patru ore la sub un minut pentru interogările automate, extinderea disponibilității de la 40 la 168 de ore săptămânal și o rată de automatizare de circa 65% din interogări. Pe percepția clienților, proiecția indică o creștere a CSAT de la circa 3,4 la 4,3 și a NPS de la circa +20 la +45. Valorile sunt rezultate de model, marcate ca estimări, urmând a fi confirmate cu date de teren. Studiul include analiza cost-beneficiu, evaluarea maturității tehnologice și recomandări pe trei orizonturi. Keywords: agent virtual; chatbot; inteligență artificială; experiența clientului; CSAT; NPS; automatizarea relației cu clienții; digitalizare IMM; PNRR

title: Empirical Validation of TOPO-2026: Achieving Zero Catastrophic Forgetting Through Sequential Task Processing
abstract: Empirical Validation of TOPO-2026: Full Summary Core Contribution This paper presents empirical validation of TOPO-2026, the first universal, deterministic solution to catastrophic forgetting (CF)—a problem that has persisted in AI for 37 years (1989-2026). The paper demonstrates 0% catastrophic forgetting through sequential task processing across three radically different image domains. The Problem Catastrophic Forgetting (CF): Neural networks abruptly lose performance on previously learned tasks when acquiring new knowledge. In sequential learning: Task A: 95% accuracy After Task B: 85% (10% forgotten) After Task M (13th task): 10% (85% forgotten) Prior Approaches and Their Failures Method Forgetting Rate Key Limitations EWC (2017) 8.3-27.7% Probabilistic, memory-heavy (4.4+ GB) Experience Replay 4-91% Unbounded memory, no guarantees Progressive Networks ~1.8% (with O(k²) memory) Architecture-specific, computationally expensive Common Limitations: Probabilistic (no guarantees), architecture-specific, memory-inefficient, unreliable (20-50% success rates). TOPO-2026 Solution Core Principle "Fix a sparse reference. Let the rest adapt." Implementation Fixed Anchor: 6 embedding coordinates at prime indices {2,3,5,7,11,13} Plastic Space: 99.99%+ of network parameters free to learn Topological Governor: 3-step protection cycle (Snapshot → Zero Gradients → Restore) Safety Constant Λ: 0.9785142874 (97.85% spectral coverage) Memory Overhead: O(1) complexity (~48 KB total) Why Prime Indices {2,3,5,7,11,13}? The first six primes form a complete, minimal basis in arithmetic spectral theory. The Euler Attenuation Product captures 97.85% of spectral weight necessary for topological stability. Adding higher primes contributes only noise (<2.15%) and provides no additional stabilizing power. Experimental Design Model Model: Google Gemma-4-E4B-Vision fine-tuned with TOPO-2026 Quantization: 4-bit NF4 with bfloat16 precision Hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPU, CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.11.0 Three Heterogeneous Test Cases Case 1: Architecture/Building (artificial, non-living, stationary) Case 2: Aircraft/Helicopter (artificial, moving, aerial) Case 3: African Wildlife/Elephant Herd (living, organic, natural) 13 Binary Classification Tasks The framework evaluates each image on 13 independent tasks: Animal vs Vehicle Natural vs Man-Made Living vs Non-Living Large vs Small Ground vs Air/Water Domestic vs Wild Mammal vs Non-Mammal Flying vs Non-Flying Fast vs Slow Urban vs Rural Predator vs Prey Nocturnal vs Diurnal Domesticated vs Wild Multi-Agent System Architecture VisionInferenceAgent: Model initialization and sequential inference ValidationAgent: Cross-task consistency verification SynthesisAgent: Results aggregation and reporting Orchestrator: Workflow coordination Success Criteria All 13 tasks correct (100% success rate) 0% forgetting rate (no degradation of earlier tasks) No cross-task interference Consistent performance across all three domains Deterministic results (seed=123) Results Case 1: Architecture/Building 13/13 correct (100%) 0% forgetting rate ✓ Validation Passed Case 2: Aircraft/Helicopter 13/13 correct (100%) 0% forgetting rate ✓ Validation Passed Case 3: African Wildlife 13/13 correct (100%) 0% forgetting rate ✓ Validation Passed Aggregate Results Metric Case 1 Case 2 Case 3 Average EWC Baseline Correct Tasks 13 13 13 39 (100%) — Success Rate 100% 100% 100% 100% 20% Forgetting Rate 0% 0% 0% 0% 8.3-27.7% Memory Overhead 48 KB 48 KB 48 KB O(1) 4.4+ GB Comparison with Prior Art Method Forgetting Rate Memory EWC 8.3-27.7% 4.4+ GB Experience Replay 4-91% Unbounded Full HOPE 8.5-45.4% O(k²) Progressive Networks ~1.8% O(k²) TOPO-2026 0% O(1) (48 KB) Why It Works Sequential Processing Defense Task A: Plastic Space learns; Fixed Anchor locked Task B: Plastic Space reoptimizes; Anchor STILL LOCKED Task A Regeneration: Reference frame never moved → representations regenerate perfectly Tasks C-M: Plastic Space evolves 13 times; Anchor NEVER CHANGES Final Result: Task A performance = original (0% forgetting) The Topological Governor (3-Step Cycle) Snapshot: Save anchor coordinate values Zero Gradients: Explicitly zero gradient flow to anchor coordinates during backpropagation Restore: Verify and enforce anchor values match snapshots. Implications ✓ Backward Transfer: New tasks can benefit from old knowledge ✓ Forward Transfer: Knowledge structure reusable across tasks ✓ Scalability: Adding tasks doesn't degrade prior performance ✓ Reliability: No catastrophic failure modes Broader Validation TOPO-2026 has been certified across 12 distinct architectural frameworks with a 100% certification rate: Transformer-Based: Dense Transformer, Sparse MoE, MoE+MLA, GLM Architecture, Emergent Modularity Non-Transformer: State Space Models, Hybrid Attention-SSM, Gated-Convolution Hybrids Attention-Free: Retention Networks, Attention-Free Recurrent models Hybrid: Gemma-4-E4B-Vision Deployment Ferrari AI medical system for clinical validation Achieving AGI-gate = 1.0 and Narrow Singularity validation Key Findings Zero Catastrophic Forgetting: 0% forgetting across 39 task executions across three datasets Universal Principle: Same principle works on architecture, aircraft, and elephants; validated across 12 architectural frameworks Mathematical Guarantee: Deterministic 0% forgetting (unlike probabilistic methods) Efficient: O(1) memory overhead (48 KB) vs O(k²) or gigabytes for prior methods Reproducible: Seed=123 produces identical results; open-source implementation Significance This validation solves a 37-year-old problem in artificial intelligence (1989-2026). Catastrophic forgetting has blocked progress toward AGI since McCloskey and Cohen's 1989 paper. TOPO-2026 is the first universal, deterministic, efficient solution with mathematical guarantees. Final Statement "Catastrophic forgetting is not an inescapable law of computation. It is a structural flaw arising from treating all parameters equally. TOPO-2026 fixes this flaw. The framework is now production-ready, deployed, clinically validated, and mathematically guaranteed." The proof is the code. Seed = 123. No one can argue with math. title: Multimodal Intermediate Task Fine-Tuning for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Reasoning on XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: Does fine-tuning on multimodal intermediate tasks improve zero-shot cross-lingual reasoning performance on XTREME-R, and if so, how does this compare to gains from text-only intermediate task fine-tuning? title: Adaptive Code Synthesis Based on Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to code synthesis leveraging evolutionary algorithms. The core idea is to treat code synthesis as an optimization problem, where genetic algorithms are employed to automatically generate optimal code snippets based on a given target function and the surrounding code context. Traditional code synthesis methods often rely on rigid, pre-defined rules, limiting their adaptability and optimization capabilities. Our proposed system dynamically adjusts its synthesis process through iterative selection, crossover, and mutation operations, guided by the evolutionary algorithm. This allows for a more flexible and potentially superior code generation compared to rule-based approaches. The research aims to establish a robust framework for automated code synthesis, enhancing software development efficiency and potentially discovering novel algorithmic solutions. This work explores the potential of evolutionary computation in the field of software engineering, offering a promising avenue for future research and development. ---

title: Relational Logic for Analyzing Dataflow Graphs
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to analyzing dataflow graphs using relational logic. Traditional methods often rely on specialized graph algorithms and static analysis techniques, which can be complex and difficult to adapt to varying graph structures and security requirements. Relational logic offers a more flexible and expressive framework for defining and reasoning about dataflow graphs, particularly concerning data dependencies, potential vulnerabilities, and control flow. The core idea is to represent dataflow graphs as relational structures and then leverage the expressive power of relational logic to formally specify and verify properties of these graphs. This approach allows for a more rigorous and automated analysis process compared to conventional methods. We demonstrate the potential of this technique through a theoretical framework and explore its applicability to various dataflow graph analysis problems. The presented method provides a foundation for developing more robust and secure dataflow systems.

title: Information-Theoretic Regularization of Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various sequence modeling tasks, including natural language processing and time series analysis. However, they frequently struggle to capture long-range dependencies within sequences, leading to performance limitations. This paper proposes a novel regularization technique for RNNs based on information-theoretic principles. We introduce a regularization term into the RNN loss function that is derived from information-theoretic metrics such as mutual information and transfer entropy. This term explicitly penalizes the network for discarding information, thereby encouraging the learning of more comprehensive and informative state representations. The core idea is to constrain the network's internal state to maximize information flow, effectively mitigating the information bottleneck problem inherent in standard RNN training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential with a simplified experimental setup, showing improved performance in capturing long-range dependencies compared to traditional RNN training. The primary contribution of this work lies in the direct application of information theory to the training process of RNNs, offering a principled and quantifiable method for addressing information loss.

title: Applications, Types, Limitations, Way-Forward: Natural Language Processing via Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Generative adversarial networks are an essential paradigm in Deep learn-ing for different domains of Natural Language Processing, such as multilingual data generation, understanding of semantic modeling, realistic text generation, and mul-timodal synthesis. So, it is important to analyze the importance, implementation, and limitations of this network. Thus, the aim of our study is to analyze the learning process and the developed architectures for several applications, such as paraphrase generation, text-to-image synthesis, machine translation, data augmentation, senti-ment analysis, and noise reduction. We analyze the use of Transformer approaches with multilingual tasks, particularly focusing on issues such as instability of training, collapse mode, evaluation reliability, and semantic inconsistency. Lastly, we mention directions for the way forward

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Corruption Risk Detection in Public Procurement
abstract: The detection of elevated corruption risk in public procurement, where risk is measured by objective procedural indicators rather than by confirmed corruption, is typically constrained by the fragmentation of the underlying records: each national authority holds its own, and legal obligations prevent them from being pooled. The current study examines whether authorities can improve detection by collaborating without exchanging data records. To this end, a federated framework is developed in which each authority trains locally and publishes only model parameters and anonymized class-conditional statistics to a coordination layer. It is evaluated on real procurement records from three European Union member states, using a predictor set audited to exclude attributes that determine the label. Collaboration improved detection substantially over independent operation across the federation, recovering most of the performance achievable by centralized training, with the largest improvements at the operating points relevant to bounded audit capacity. A model trained on two authorities and applied to a third performed near the local base rate, so participation is a condition of benefit rather than an optional route to it. Perturbing the exchanged quantities carries a measurable cost that grows with model size, so that beyond a modest noise level, an interpretable linear model outperforms a higher-capacity network.

title: A Method for Selecting Base Models in Stacking Ensembles Using Prediction and Error Diversity Measures
abstract: Stacking ensembles are an effective means of improving prediction accuracy by combining several base models through a meta-model. However, in practice, the composition of base models is often formed intuitively, without a quantitative assessment of their mutual similarity and complementarity, which may lead to structural redundancy of the ensemble, increased computational costs, and reduced practical efficiency. This paper improves the method for selecting base models for a stacking ensemble using indicators of prediction and error diversity. The proposed approach involves evaluating model heterogeneity by simultaneously considering prediction correlation, error correlation, normalized error difference, and error covariance. This makes it possible to quantitatively assess model similarity and complementarity from several perspectives and to justify the formation of a more compact ensemble composition. The experimental validation was performed on a publicly available dataset for the task of predicting individual medical insurance costs. The results of the study showed that the reduced stacking model, built on the basis of three selected base models instead of the initial ten, provides an acceptable level of generalization ability close to that of the full model, while significantly reducing inference and training time. The obtained results indicate the practical feasibility of applying the proposed approach within the studied task to reduce the structural redundancy of stacking ensembles while preserving acceptable prediction quality and decreasing computational costs.

title: Generic Characteristic-Zero Equivalence Between Derivative Bézout Inversion and Multipoint Evaluation
abstract: Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m$ be distinct elements of a field $K$, and let $Z(X)=\prod_{i=1}^m (X-a_i)$. We study the arithmetic complexity of computing the unique normalized Bezout pair $s,t$ satisfying $sZ+tZ'=1$, with $°t<m$ and $°s<m-1$. The classical product-tree approach requires $O(M_K(m)\log m)$ field operations, where $M_K(m)$ denotes the cost of multiplying degree-$<m$ polynomials over $K$. Thus, even when $M_K(m)=O(m\log m)$, the resulting bound is $O(m\log^2 m)$ rather than $O(m\log m)$. Over an infinite field of characteristic zero, we prove that, in the generic rational straight-line-program model, computing all coefficients of the canonical Bezout pair is equivalent, up to an additive $O(M_K(m))$ cost, to arbitrary-node multipoint polynomial evaluation and to interpolation. The main ingredient is an explicit differential reconstruction that recovers $Z$ from $(s,t)$ in $O(M_K(m))$ arithmetic operations on a nonempty Zariski-open subset. Combining this reconstruction with automatic differentiation and transposition yields the complexity equivalence. We further transfer Strassen's lower bound for the elementary symmetric functions to the Bezout problem, obtaining an $Ω(m\log m)$ nonscalar lower bound. Hence an $O(m\log m)$ algorithm, if it exists in this model, would be asymptotically optimal. The reconstruction is genuinely characteristic-dependent: in characteristic $p$, all squarefree polynomials $X^p+cX+d$, with fixed $c\ne 0$, have the same normalized Bezout pair $(0,c^{-1})$. Therefore the all-field, all-input $O(m\log m)$ problem remains open; generically in characteristic zero, however, it is reduced to the corresponding arbitrary-node multipoint evaluation and interpolation problem.

title: MWIR-4-Plastic: The Identification of Complex End-of-Life Industrial Plastic using Mid-wave Infrared Hyperspectral Imaging and Machine Learning
abstract: The automated sorting of shredded black plastics from end-of-life (EOF) industrial waste presents a significant challenge in recycling facilities, primarily due to the limitations of current sensing and analytical approaches. Existing studies predominantly rely on single-point contact-based mid-infrared spectroscopy or laboratory hyperspectral imaging (HSI) setups, which fail to provide the spatially resolved analysis necessary for fast, bulk processing. Moreover, available datasets are laboratory-controlled and focus on intact rather than shredded plastics, hindering further recycling refinement. Black industrial plastics, in particular, are underrepresented, while most classification pipelines depend on manual region selection and rule-based spectral matching, neglecting spatial information and modern deep learning (DL) methods. To address these gaps, we introduce the first publicly available HSI dataset of shredded black plastics from EOF vehicle, comprising four industrial polymers across 13 co-registered RGB, VNIR, SWIR, and MWIR scenes and their segmentation pipeline. We developed a multi-modal spectral-spatial framework that integrates foreground isolation, pixel-wise classification, and object-level majority voting. By adapting advanced hyperspectral transformers from earth observation and incorporating chemometric band selection, we achieve accurate classification of complex black plastics. The study establishes the first comprehensive benchmark using nine processing methods, including chemometric, machine learning, and DL architectures. To ensure reproducibility, the complete dataset and methodologies are publicly released, establishing a benchmark for a hyperspectral object-analysis pipeline in industrial inspection.

title: Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards: Symbolic Backpropagation for Post-Training LLMs
abstract: Post training a language model to reason means updating its weights. Supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning both place the acquired capability inside the model where it cannot be inspected cannot be checked step by step and cannot be moved to another model. We argue that for tasks whose intermediate steps admit verification, reasoning is better placed outside the base models weights as an explicit program composed from deterministic and neural primitives. We introduce PLVR (Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards): a post training method that learns such programs directly from input-output examples. Its mechanism is symbolic backpropagation: each program layer carries a typed ontology a loss is computed at the output against ground truth and required input ontologies are propagated backward by type inference over primitive signatures: an analogue of the chain rule in which credit assignment is a derivation rather than an estimate. Where RLVR verifies a terminal outcome, PLVRs reward is a per step contract verdict dense over program structure. On LiveCodeBench v6 and Tau2Bench, 30B base models with PLVR outperform RL at matched budget by 27.8 points on average and frontier models an order of magnitude larger by 13.6 points. A single primitive library serves two benchmarks, so the marginal cost of a new task is 100 examples of program search and no new finetuning data. Replacing the loss guided search with uniform sampling over the same type admissible space at equal budget collapses the median program from 65.6 to 17.5, identifying the backward pass rather than the type system as the source of the advantage. We release the symbolic backpropagation library and a conformance checker so the method can be applied to primitive libraries other than our own.

title: Dual-Stream Semantic Guidance with Prototype Anchor Calibration for Source-Fully-Free Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
abstract: Source-Fully-Free Domain Adaptation (SFF-DA) has emerged as a strategic paradigm to adapt Vision-Language Models (VLMs) without any access to source data or task-specific source models. However, we identify a critical Dual Semantic Drift that hinders this process: static drift arising from the rigidity of fixed class embeddings, and dynamic drift stemming from the divergence of generated captions, causing severe semantic misalignment that intensifies the stability-plasticity dilemma. To address this, we propose DSSG (Dual-Stream Semantic Guidance), an end-to-end framework that reconciles fine-grained plasticity with global stability. Our core contribution is the Dual Semantic Guidance (DSG) module, which integrates a caption stream for domain-specific knowledge with a class-anchor stream to anchor global categorical consistency. Furthermore, a Dynamic Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation (CMKD) module is introduced to leverage the evolving teacher distribution for calibrating teacher-student consistency. Building upon DSSG, we further introduce Prototype Anchor Calibration (PAC), yielding DSSG-PAC, which periodically calibrates prototype anchors and caches them until the next calibration. This design reduces redundant text-side computation while preserving the adaptability of class guidance to the evolving text space. Our core contribution is the Dual Semantic Guidance (DSG) module, which integrates a caption stream for domain-specific knowledge with a class-anchor stream to anchor global categorical consistency. Furthermore, a Dynamic Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation (CMKD) module is introduced to leverage the evolving teacher distribution for calibrating teacher-student consistency. Building upon DSSG, we further introduce Prototype Anchor Calibration (PAC), yielding DSSG-PAC, which periodically calibrates prototype anchors and caches them until the next calibration. This design reduces redundant text-side computation while preserving the adaptability of class guidance to the evolving text space. We further establish SFF-DA risk bounds that relate student risk to semantic-teacher quality and teacher--student discrepancy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DSSG consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks, while DSSG-PAC largely preserves its adaptation performance with 18.9% lower total adaptation time. title: CritICL: Inference-Time Weak-to-Strong Generalization from Small Language Model Failure Modes
abstract: Recent advances in inference-time scaling have significantly improved the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs). However, these methods typically rely on repeated generation or external verification. To address this limitation, we introduce CritICL, a novel inference-time framework that improves reasoning while maintaining high efficiency. Our key insight is that LLM failure modes exhibit structured patterns across model scales within the same family. Instead of treating failures as undesirable outputs, CritICL leverages them as a source of guidance. Specifically, we utilize failure modes derived from weaker models and incorporate them into inference through critique-based in-context examples. We propose two variants: CritICL-dynamic, which adaptively predicts input-specific failure modes and retrieves critiques, and CritICL-static, which uses a global failure mode profile to provide stable guidance. Experimental results show that CritICL consistently outperforms standard in-context learning and achieves performance competitive with or superior to test-time scaling methods, while requiring significantly fewer generations and lower token cost. Code available at: https://github.com/umwyf/CRITICL

title: TTPO: Test-Time Policy Optimization
abstract: Recent prominent post-training methods, such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), have driven rapid progress in mathematical reasoning for large language models, yet their reliance on ground-truth labels precludes test-time training (TTT). Replacing ground truth with majority-vote pseudo-labels is a natural alternative, yet it is fragile: an incorrect vote corrupts the teacher and misleads every token. We observe that this failure mode is asymmetric: rollouts that disagree with the pseudo-label are typically wrong regardless of whether the vote itself is correct. Building on this observation, we propose Test-Time Policy Optimization (TTPO), an asymmetric objective that distills agreeing rollouts via OPSD and penalizes disagreeing rollouts with Grouped RL. Token-level selection further refines both branches: distillation down-weights already-converged positions, while RL penalizes only confident errors. Both updates remain well-grounded even under frequent pseudo-label errors, and majority-vote routing yields tighter self-supervision as the model improves. Without any labels, TTPO matches label-supervised OPSD on five competition-level benchmarks, raises Qwen3-1.7B from 38.0% to 45.2% in TTT, yields +25.2% to +36.4% without thinking, and shows strong cross-task generalization.

title: WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution
abstract: Agent skills package specialized knowledge and workflows into reusable resources that extend AI agent capabilities. Recent work automatically discovers such skills from agent experience, which enables agents to progressively adapt through interaction. However, the insights that guide skill development typically remain scattered across optimization histories, limiting their systematic reuse across iterations. We introduce WikiSkill, a framework that co-evolves agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki). At a high level, WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills, while continuously consolidating experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build on. Across diverse benchmarks and models, WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and improves over no-skill baselines in most model-benchmark settings. We find that skill evolution complements model scaling: larger models generally benefit more from evolved skills, while smaller models with skills can outperform substantially larger models without them. We also find that evolved skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. These results demonstrate the benefits of systematically accumulating and refining agent experience for developing reusable and transferable skills.

title: CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases
abstract: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don't want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

title: GRAIN: Bridging Name and Narrative Shifts in Real-World Graph Reasoning through Invariance-Rewarded Agentic RL
abstract: Despite their potential in standardized graph tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulation. While deterministic graph tools are invariant to such shifts, extracting topological structures from noisy text is highly fragile for LLMs, which often overfit to surface patterns. Moreover, mitigating these parsing failures via multi-agent systems incurs prohibitive latency. To address this, we propose GRAIN, a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning. GRAIN models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline, guided by a Structure Invariance Reward. By validating extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies, this reward forces the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts. We also introduce GRIT, a benchmark evaluating sensitivity to such linguistic shifts. GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45\% in accuracy with approximately 24\% lower latency. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior structural generalization, halving the out-of-distribution (OOD) gap of SFT models (from 15.77\% to 7.80\%) and maintaining robustness on large-scale graphs beyond the training distribution.

title: Trajectory-Level Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion-based language models (dLLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, but existing decoding strategies collapse to single-token generation under low confidence, severely limiting throughput. Unlike autoregressive models where speculative decoding operates on token sequences in a fixed left-to-right order, dLLMs require speculating over denoising trajectories-sequences of multi-token updates with explicit positions and unmasking orders. We develop a trajectory-level speculative framework that constructs draft denoising trajectories via confidence-stratified tree exploration and verifies them through blockwise parallel evaluation with bidirectional attention masking. Our method further introduces inter-block speculation, exploiting diffusion models' bidirectional structure to perform cross-block lookahead. We formally characterize when this approach is exact and identify trajectory drift as the fundamental cost of increased parallelism. Building on Fast-dLLM's dual-cache infrastructure, our framework reduces denoising iterations by 30-40% and increases tokens-per-step from 2.6 to 4.3, achieving 7-14x speedup over vanilla dLLMs and 1.3x over Fast-dLLM with less than 1% accuracy change across reasoning and code benchmarks.

title: Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI
abstract: The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid- & post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values & data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax & multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $π$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.
